objectives.statement: Convert between millimetres, centimetres, metres and kilometres, between grams and kilograms, and between millilitres and litres.
Convert between mm$^2$, cm$^2$, m$^2$ and km$^2$, and between mm$^3$, cm$^3$ and m$^3$, using the fact that an area factor is the length factor squared and a volume factor is the length factor cubed.
Convert between volume and capacity (cm$^3\leftrightarrow$ml, m$^3\leftrightarrow$litres).
Choose sensible units for a practical measurement, convert all lengths to the same unit before calculating an area or volume, and give an answer in the unit requested.

prerequisites.statement: Multiply and divide a number by 10, 100 and 1000 (and other powers of 10) mentally.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every metric conversion in this lesson is exactly a multiplication or division by a power of 10 (or, for area and volume, by that power of 10 squared or cubed); without fast, confident recall of this skill every conversion becomes a slow, error-prone calculation.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise that the area of a square of side 1 unit is exactly 1 square unit.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Seeing why 1 m$^2$ is a square of side 100 cm, and therefore holds $100\times100$ unit squares of 1 cm$^2$, is the entire justification for squaring the length factor when converting areas; without this picture, 'square the conversion factor' is just a rule to memorise, not something understood.

prerequisites.statement: Multiply and divide decimals, including decimals less than 1.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Several conversions in this lesson go from a larger unit to a smaller one and back (e.g. 250 g to kg, 0.85 L to ml), and these routinely produce or start from decimals.

prerequisites.statement: Find the volume of a cuboid as length × width × height.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Several of this lesson's context problems (a tank, a swimming pool, rainfall on a roof) ask for a volume in one unit system before converting it to another; without the cuboid volume formula itself, there is nothing yet to convert.

diagnostic_items.question: Why is $1\,\text{m}^2$ equal to $10\,000\,\text{cm}^2$ and not $100\,\text{cm}^2$?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Because area counts squares, not lengths. A square of side 1 m has sides of 100 cm, so it contains $100\times100=10\,000$ squares of side 1 cm, not 100 of them.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Because $1\,\text{m}=100\,\text{cm}$, so $1\,\text{m}^2=100\,\text{cm}^2$.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Applies the LENGTH conversion factor directly to an area, without squaring it — the single most common error in this lesson.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks whether the learner has genuinely understood why an area factor must be squared, or is only repeating 'square the factor' as an unexplained rule.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Draw a 1 m by 1 m square subdivided into a 100-by-100 grid of 1 cm squares, and count rows × columns explicitly: $100\times100=10\,000$, not $100$.

diagnostic_items.question: How many millilitres are there in one cubic metre?

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Converts $\text{m}^3$ to litres correctly but stops there, forgetting the second conversion from litres to millilitres.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Tests whether the learner can chain two conversions ($\text{m}^3\to$ litres $\to$ ml) rather than stopping after the first step.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Write the chain explicitly as two separate equalities on one line: $1\,\text{m}^3=1000\,\ell=1000\times1000\,\text{ml}=1\,000\,000\,\text{ml}$, so no step is skipped.

diagnostic_items.question: You convert $3\,\text{cm}^2$ to $\text{mm}^2$ and get $30\,\text{mm}^2$. Is this reasonable? Explain.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: No. $1\,\text{cm}^2=10^2=100\,\text{mm}^2$ (not 10), so $3\,\text{cm}^2=300\,\text{mm}^2$. The answer $30$ used the LENGTH factor (10) instead of the area factor (100).

common_wrong_answers.answer: Yes, because $1\,\text{cm}=10\,\text{mm}$, so $3\,\text{cm}^2\times10=30\,\text{mm}^2$ looks right.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Accepts the answer because the arithmetic step 'looks like' a conversion, without checking that the CORRECT factor (squared) was used.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Tests whether the learner can catch someone else's error — a stronger skill than just not making the error themselves — by checking the factor used, not just the arithmetic.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Ask: 'is this an area conversion or a length conversion?' first, then look up the matching factor (100, not 10) before judging the arithmetic.

diagnostic_items.question: Which is bigger, $0.5\,\text{m}^3$ or $400\,\ell$?

common_wrong_answers.answer: $400\,\ell$, because $400$ is a bigger number than $0.5$.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Compares the two raw numbers without first converting them to the same unit — the two quantities cannot be compared at all until they share a unit.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks that the learner converts to a common unit BEFORE comparing two quantities, rather than comparing the numbers as given.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: State explicitly: 'you cannot compare two measurements until they are in the same unit', then convert $0.5\,\text{m}^3$ to litres first.

theory_blocks.title: One idea: length, area, volume scale differently
theory_blocks.body: A length conversion multiplies by the scale factor $k$ between two units. An area conversion multiplies by [[blue:$k^2$]], and a volume conversion by [[blue:$k^3$]], because area counts squares and volume counts cubes. Since $1\,\text{m}=100\,\text{cm}$, this one idea gives $1\,\text{m}^2=100^2=10\,000\,\text{cm}^2$ and $1\,\text{m}^3=100^3=1\,000\,000\,\text{cm}^3$ — every conversion fact in this lesson comes from applying it consistently.
