theory_blocks.title: Units of length, mass and capacity
theory_blocks.body:
The metric system is based on powers of 10. The prefixes are worth knowing: *kilo* $=1000$, *centi* $=\tfrac1{100}$, *milli* $=\tfrac1{1000}$.

| Quantity | Units | Conversions |
|---|---|---|
| Length | mm, cm, m, km | $1\,\text{cm}=10\,\text{mm}$, $1\,\text{m}=100\,\text{cm}$, $1\,\text{km}=1000\,\text{m}$ |
| Mass | g, kg (and tonne) | $1\,\text{kg}=1000\,\text{g}$, $1\,\text{tonne}=1000\,\text{kg}$ |
| Capacity | ml, L | $1\,\ell=1000\,\text{ml}$ |

theory_blocks.title: Bigger number or smaller number?
theory_blocks.body: Going to a SMALLER unit? You need MORE of them, so multiply. Going to a LARGER unit? You need FEWER, so divide. Ask yourself first: 'should my number get bigger or smaller?' — decide this before doing any arithmetic.

theory_blocks.title: Units of area: squaring the length factor
theory_blocks.body:
Area counts *squares*, so the conversion factor is the length factor **squared**. A square of side 1 m, measured in centimetres, has sides of 100 cm, so it contains $100\times100=10\,000$ squares of side 1 cm: $1\,\text{m}^2=10\,000\,\text{cm}^2$.

Chaining the length factors gives every area factor: $1\,\text{km}^2=1000^2=1\,000\,000\,\text{m}^2$, $1\,\text{m}^2=100^2=10\,000\,\text{cm}^2$, $1\,\text{cm}^2=10^2=100\,\text{mm}^2$.

theory_blocks.title: The classic error: forgetting to square (or cube)
theory_blocks.body: Writing $1\,\text{m}^2=100\,\text{cm}^2$ is wrong: $100$ is the LENGTH conversion factor. For area it must be [[blue:squared]]: $1\,\text{m}^2=100\times100=10\,000\,\text{cm}^2$. The same error with volume gives $1\,\text{m}^3=100\,\text{cm}^3$ instead of the correct $1\,000\,000\,\text{cm}^3$.

theory_blocks.title: Units of volume, and the link to capacity
theory_blocks.body:
Volume counts *cubes*, so the factor is the length factor **cubed**: $1\,\text{cm}^3=10^3=1000\,\text{mm}^3$ and $1\,\text{m}^3=100^3=1\,000\,000\,\text{cm}^3$.

**Capacity** (how much a container holds) is measured in millilitres and litres. The single most useful fact linking the two systems: a cube of side 10 cm holds exactly one litre, because $10\times10\times10=1000\,\text{cm}^3$.
$$1\,\text{ml}=1\,\text{cm}^3,\qquad 1\,\ell=1000\,\text{cm}^3,\qquad 1\,\text{m}^3=1000\,\ell.$$
The last equation follows because $1\,\text{m}^3=1\,000\,000\,\text{cm}^3$ and $1\,000\,000\div1000=1000$ litres.

theory_blocks.title: Same unit before you calculate
theory_blocks.body: Before calculating an area or a volume, put ALL the lengths in the SAME unit. A rectangle 2 m by 50 cm has area $200\times50=10\,000\,\text{cm}^2$ (or $2\times0.5=1\,\text{m}^2$) — never $2\times50=100$.

theory_blocks.title: Sense checks for everyday measurements
theory_blocks.body: Keep a few everyday sizes in mind to catch an obviously wrong conversion: a door is about 2 m high; a cup holds about 250 ml; a can of drink has a mass of about 350 g; a classroom floor is about $50\,\text{m}^2$. If an answer says a cup holds 250 litres, the wrong conversion factor has been used somewhere.

keywords.definition: The system of measurement based on powers of 10, using prefixes such as kilo-, centi- and milli-.
A one-dimensional measurement, in units such as mm, cm, m or km.
The amount of matter in an object, measured in grams, kilograms or tonnes.
How much a container holds, measured in millilitres or litres.
The amount of flat surface covered by a shape, measured in square units such as $\text{cm}^2$ or $\text{m}^2$.
The amount of space occupied by a solid, measured in cubic units such as $\text{cm}^3$ or $\text{m}^3$.
The number you multiply or divide by to change a measurement from one unit to another.
A unit of capacity equal to $1000\,\text{cm}^3$.
The ratio by which a length, area or volume is multiplied when converting between units or enlarging a shape.

worked_examples.statement: Length, mass and capacity. Convert (a) $3.4$ km to metres; (b) $250$ g to kilograms; (c) $0.85$ L to millilitres; (d) $72$ mm to centimetres.
reasoning: (a) Metres are smaller than kilometres, so multiply: $3.4\times1000=3400$.
(b) Kilograms are larger than grams, so divide: $250\div1000=0.25$.
(c) Millilitres are smaller than litres, so multiply: $0.85\times1000=850$.
(d) Centimetres are larger than millimetres, so divide: $72\div10=7.2$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Deciding the direction (multiply or divide) before doing any arithmetic, by comparing the sizes of the two units, avoids the single most common error in this lesson.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Dividing in (a) and (c), or multiplying in (b) and (d), by applying the 'multiply' habit from earlier, easier examples without checking which unit is actually larger each time.

worked_examples.statement: Area conversions. (a) Convert $2.5\,\text{m}^2$ to $\text{cm}^2$. (b) Convert $45\,000\,\text{cm}^2$ to $\text{m}^2$. (c) Convert $350\,\text{mm}^2$ to $\text{cm}^2$.
reasoning: (a) Going to a smaller unit, multiply by the AREA factor $100^2=10\,000$: $2.5\times10\,000=25\,000$.
(b) Going to a larger unit, divide by $10\,000$: $45\,000\div10\,000=4.5$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Each part uses the SQUARED length factor for the pair of units involved, confirming the rule of the related idea in three different directions.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Using the length factor 100 in part (a) instead of the area factor $10\,000$, giving $250$ instead of $25\,000$.

worked_examples.statement: Volume and capacity. (a) Convert $0.8\,\text{m}^3$ to litres. (b) A jug holds $2.4$ litres: what is its capacity in $\text{cm}^3$? (c) A rectangular tank measures $1.2$ m by $80$ cm by $50$ cm. How many litres does it hold?
unknowns: capacity in litres or $\text{cm}^3$ in each part
reasoning: (c) The units are mixed, so first write every length in centimetres: $1.2\,\text{m}=120\,\text{cm}$. Volume $=120\times80\times50=480\,000\,\text{cm}^3$, then divide by 1000 to reach litres: $480\,000\div1000=480$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Part (c) is the first example combining two separate skills: converting mixed units to a common one BEFORE multiplying, then converting the resulting volume to capacity.
worked_examples.common_mistake: In part (c), multiplying $1.2\times80\times50$ directly without converting the 1.2 m to centimetres first, mixing metres and centimetres in the same product.

worked_examples.statement: Tiling. A floor $6$ m by $4.5$ m is covered with square tiles of side $30$ cm. How many tiles are needed?
reasoning: Method 1, in centimetres: the floor is $600$ cm by $450$ cm, fitting $600\div30=20$ tiles along one side and $450\div30=15$ along the other: $20\times15=300$.
Method 2, with areas: floor $=6\times4.5=27\,\text{m}^2=270\,000\,\text{cm}^2$; one tile is $30\times30=900\,\text{cm}^2$; $270\,000\div900=300$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Checking a result by two genuinely different methods (counting rows/columns vs. dividing total areas) is a powerful way to catch a unit-conversion slip before it reaches a final answer.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Mixing units within Method 2 by forgetting to convert the floor's area from $\text{m}^2$ to $\text{cm}^2$ before dividing by the tile's area in $\text{cm}^2$.

worked_examples.statement: Rainfall. During a storm, $15$ mm of rain falls on a flat roof $8$ m by $5$ m. How many litres of water land on the roof?
reasoning: The fallen water forms a thin cuboid of base $8\times5=40\,\text{m}^2$ and height $15\,\text{mm}=0.015\,\text{m}$, all converted to metres first.
worked_examples.interpretation: Reading '15 mm of rain' as a HEIGHT turns an unfamiliar weather fact into an ordinary cuboid-volume problem, provided the mm depth is converted to metres to match the roof's dimensions first.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Leaving the rainfall depth in millimetres while the roof's sides are in metres, multiplying $8\times5\times15$ directly and producing a volume with no consistent unit.

guided_exercises.statement: Convert: (a) $5.2$ km to m; (b) $630$ g to kg; (c) $1800$ ml to litres.
hints: Decide first, for each part, whether the new unit is smaller or larger than the one given.
Smaller unit → multiply; larger unit → divide.
guided_exercises.full_solution: (a) Metres are smaller than kilometres: $5.2\times1000=5200$ m. (b) Kilograms are larger than grams: $630\div1000=0.63$ kg. (c) Litres are larger than millilitres: $1800\div1000=1.8$ litres.
common_errors: Dividing in (a) instead of multiplying, from assuming every conversion involving a '1000' factor must be a division.

guided_exercises.statement: A square plot of land has area $3.6\,\text{m}^2$. A planner needs this area in $\text{cm}^2$ to compare it with a scale drawing marked in centimetres. Convert $3.6\,\text{m}^2$ to $\text{cm}^2$.
hints: This is an AREA conversion, not a length conversion: the factor between m and cm must be squared, not used as it is.
guided_exercises.full_solution: The length factor from m to cm is $100$; for area this becomes $100^2=10\,000$. So $3.6\,\text{m}^2=3.6\times10\,000=36\,000\,\text{cm}^2$.
common_errors: Multiplying by $100$ instead of $10\,000$, giving $360$ instead of $36\,000$ — the length-factor-for-area error (the related idea).

guided_exercises.statement: An aquarium is a cuboid $50$ cm long, $30$ cm wide and $40$ cm high. Find its capacity in litres.
hints: Find the volume first, in cubic centimetres, using length × width × height.
Then convert the volume from $\text{cm}^3$ to litres, using $1\,\ell=1000\,\text{cm}^3$.
common_errors: Dividing by $100$ instead of $1000$ in the final step, confusing the cm–m length factor with the $\text{cm}^3$–litre volume factor.

exercises.statement: Convert: (a) $3.6$ km to m; (b) $450$ cm to m; (c) $0.75$ kg to g; (d) $2500$ ml to L; (e) $7.2$ cm to mm.
exercises.full_solution: Each part applies the correct length/mass/capacity factor in the correct direction: (a) $3.6\times1000=3600$. (b) $450\div100=4.5$. (c) $0.75\times1000=750$. (d) $2500\div1000=2.5$. (e) $7.2\times10=72$.
common_errors: Dividing instead of multiplying in (a), (c) or (e), by not checking first whether the target unit is smaller or larger.

exercises.statement: Convert: (a) $4\,\text{m}^2$ to $\text{cm}^2$; (b) $60\,000\,\text{cm}^2$ to $\text{m}^2$; (c) $8\,\text{cm}^2$ to $\text{mm}^2$; (d) $2.5\,\text{km}^2$ to $\text{m}^2$; (e) $350\,\text{mm}^2$ to $\text{cm}^2$.
common_errors: Using the un-squared length factor throughout (e.g. $100$, $10$ or $1000$ instead of $10\,000$, $100$ or $1\,000\,000$) — see the related idea.

exercises.statement: Convert: (a) $3\,\text{m}^3$ to $\text{cm}^3$; (b) $5000\,\text{cm}^3$ to litres; (c) $1.75$ litres to $\text{cm}^3$; (d) $0.6\,\text{m}^3$ to litres; (e) $750$ ml to $\text{cm}^3$.
common_errors: Using the AREA factor ($10\,000$) instead of the VOLUME factor ($1\,000\,000$) in part (a) — see the related idea.

exercises.statement: A floor $6$ m by $4.5$ m is to be covered with square tiles of side $50$ cm. How many tiles are needed?
exercises.full_solution: Convert the floor to centimetres: $600\,\text{cm}\times450\,\text{cm}$. Tiles along each side: $600\div50=12$ and $450\div50=9$, so $12\times9=108$.
common_errors: Dividing the floor's area in $\text{m}^2$ directly by the tile's side length in cm, mixing two different units in one division.

exercises.statement: A fish tank is a cuboid $60$ cm by $40$ cm by $35$ cm. Find its capacity in litres.
common_errors: Dividing by $100$ instead of $1000$, confusing the length factor with the volume–capacity factor.

exercises.statement: A bottle holds $330$ ml. How many bottles can be completely filled from $5$ litres of juice?
exercises.full_solution: $5$ litres $=5000$ ml. $5000\div330=15.15\ldots$, so only $15$ whole bottles can be completely filled.
common_errors: Rounding $15.15$ up to $16$, forgetting that a PARTIALLY filled bottle does not count as 'completely filled'.

exercises.statement: A sheet of paper measures $21.0$ cm by $29.7$ cm. Find its area in $\text{m}^2$, correct to $3$ significant figures.
common_errors: Dividing by $100$ instead of $10\,000$, because the length factor (100) rather than the area factor was recalled.

exercises.statement: Twelve identical bars of chocolate have a total mass of $1.5$ kg. Find the mass of one bar in grams.
common_errors: Dividing $1.5$ by $12$ first and forgetting to convert the result to grams, leaving the answer in kilograms.

exercises.statement: $12$ mm of rain falls on a flat roof $6$ m by $4.5$ m. How many litres of water is this?
exercises.full_solution: Convert $12$ mm to $0.012$ m. Volume $=6\times4.5\times0.012=0.324\,\text{m}^3=324$ litres.
common_errors: Leaving the rainfall depth in millimetres while the roof's sides are in metres, multiplying lengths in two different units together.

exercises.statement: Write these areas in order, smallest first: $0.5\,\text{m}^2$, $4500\,\text{cm}^2$, $60\,000\,\text{mm}^2$.
exercises.full_solution: Convert all three to the same unit, say $\text{m}^2$: $60\,000\,\text{mm}^2=600\,\text{cm}^2=0.06\,\text{m}^2$; $4500\,\text{cm}^2=0.45\,\text{m}^2$; the third is already $0.5\,\text{m}^2$. Ordering: $0.06<0.45<0.5$.
common_errors: Comparing the raw numbers $0.5$, $4500$ and $60\,000$ directly, without first converting every area to a common unit.

exercises.statement: A cube has side $2.5$ m. Find its volume in litres.
common_errors: Computing $2.5\times3=7.5$ instead of $2.5^3$, confusing cubing a length with multiplying it by 3.

exercises.statement: A swimming pool is a cuboid $25$ m long, $10$ m wide and $1.8$ m deep. It is filled by a hose delivering $150$ litres per minute. How many hours does it take to fill the pool?
exercises.full_solution: Volume $=25\times10\times1.8=450\,\text{m}^3=450\,000$ litres. Time $=450\,000\div150=3000$ minutes $=3000\div60=50$ hours.
common_errors: Forgetting the final conversion from minutes to hours, leaving the answer as $3000$.

exercises.statement: On a map with scale $1:50\,000$, an area of $1\,\text{cm}^2$ on the map represents how many $\text{km}^2$ on the ground?
exercises.full_solution: $1$ cm on the map is $50\,000$ cm on the ground, which is $0.5$ km. The AREA scale factor is the length scale factor squared: $0.5^2=0.25\,\text{km}^2$.
common_errors: Using the length scale factor $50\,000$ (or $0.5$) directly as the area factor, without squaring it — see the related idea.

exercises.statement: A cuboid measures $0.4$ m by $25$ cm by $200$ mm. Find its volume in litres.
exercises.full_solution: Convert every length to cm: $0.4\,\text{m}=40\,\text{cm}$, $25\,\text{cm}$, $200\,\text{mm}=20\,\text{cm}$. Volume $=40\times25\times20=20\,000\,\text{cm}^3=20$ litres.
common_errors: Multiplying $0.4\times25\times200$ directly, mixing metres, centimetres and millimetres in a single product.

exercises.statement: One litre of paint covers $12\,\text{m}^2$. A wall $3.5$ m by $2.4$ m needs two coats. How many litres of paint are needed?
exercises.full_solution: Area $=3.5\times2.4=8.4\,\text{m}^2$. Two coats need $16.8\,\text{m}^2$ of coverage. Litres needed $=16.8\div12=1.4$.
common_errors: Forgetting to double the area for the two coats, giving $0.7$ instead of $1.4$.

exercises.statement: Write $1\,\text{m}^3$ in $\text{mm}^3$, in standard form.
common_errors: Cubing $1000$ incorrectly as $3000$ or $1\,000\,000$, instead of $1000^3=10^9$.

exam_questions.statement:
A fish tank is a cuboid measuring $45$ cm by $30$ cm by $25$ cm.
(a) Calculate the capacity of the tank, in litres. [3]
(b) The tank is filled with water to a depth of $20$ cm. Calculate the number of litres of water in the tank at this depth. [2]
(c) Calculate how many more litres of water are needed to fill the tank completely. [2]
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) Volume $=45\times30\times25=33\,750\,\text{cm}^3$; since $1\,\ell=1000\,\text{cm}^3$, this is $33.75$ litres. (b) Volume at depth $20$: $45\times30\times20=27\,000\,\text{cm}^3=27$ litres. (c) $33.75-27=6.75$ litres.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for the volume $45\times30\times25$; A1 for $33\,750\,\text{cm}^3$; B1 for converting to $33.75$ litres (dividing by $1000$)
(b) M1 for $45\times30\times20=27\,000$; A1 for $27$ litres
(c) M1 (dep. on (a) and (b)) for subtracting; A1 for $6.75$ litres (follow through on their values from (a) and (b)).
common_errors: In (a), dividing by $100$ instead of $1000$ when converting $\text{cm}^3$ to litres.

exam_questions.statement:
(a) Write down the number of $\text{cm}^2$ in $1\,\text{m}^2$. [1]
(b) A square tabletop has area $3.2\,\text{m}^2$. Find the length of one side of the tabletop in centimetres, correct to $3$ significant figures. [3]
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) $1\,\text{m}=100\,\text{cm}$, so $1\,\text{m}^2=100^2=10\,000\,\text{cm}^2$. (b) The side length in metres is $\sqrt{3.2}=1.78885\ldots$ m; converting to cm: $1.78885\ldots\times100=178.885\ldots\approx179$ cm (3 s.f.).
mark_scheme: (b) M1 for $\sqrt{3.2}$ (or $\sqrt{32\,000}$); M1 for converting the unrounded square root to centimetres (multiplying by $100$); A1 for $179$ cm (3 s.f.).
common_errors: Converting $3.2\,\text{m}^2$ to $320\,\text{cm}^2$ (using the length factor 100 instead of 10 000) before taking the square root, giving $\sqrt{320}\approx17.9$ cm — a side length ten times too small.

exam_questions.statement:
Rainwater collects on the flat roof of a garden shed. The roof measures $2.4$ m by $1.8$ m. During a storm, $8$ mm of rain falls on the roof.
(a) Calculate the volume of water that falls on the roof, giving your answer in $\text{m}^3$. [2]
(b) Convert your answer to part (a) into litres. [1]
(c) The water drains into a container that already holds $10$ litres. The container has a maximum capacity of $40$ litres. Does the container overflow? Show your working. [2]
exam_questions.answer: (a) $0.034\,56\,\text{m}^3$ (b) $34.56$ litres (c) Yes; $10+34.56=44.56>40$, so the container overflows.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) Convert the rainfall depth to metres: $8\,\text{mm}=0.008\,\text{m}$. Volume $=2.4\times1.8\times0.008=0.034\,56\,\text{m}^3$. (b) $0.034\,56\times1000=34.56$ litres. (c) Total $=10+34.56=44.56$ litres, which is MORE than the $40$-litre capacity, so the container overflows.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for converting $8$ mm to $0.008$ m; A1 for $0.034\,56\,\text{m}^3$ (accept equivalent correct unrounded form)
(b) B1 for $34.56$ litres (follow through on their (a))
(c) M1 for adding $10$ to their (b); A1 for the conclusion 'it overflows' with a correct comparison against $40$ shown.
common_errors: Multiplying $2.4\times1.8\times8$ without converting the millimetre depth to metres first, producing a volume with inconsistent units.

challenge_questions.statement: A student says: '$1\,\text{km}=1000\,\text{m}$, so $1\,\text{km}^2=1000\,\text{m}^2$.' Explain the error and find the number of $\text{m}^2$ in $1\,\text{km}^2$, then in $0.03\,\text{km}^2$.
challenge_questions.answer: The student forgot to square the length factor. $1\,\text{km}^2=1\,000\,000\,\text{m}^2$; $0.03\,\text{km}^2=30\,000\,\text{m}^2$.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Area scales by the SQUARE of the length factor, not the length factor itself: $1\,\text{km}^2=1000\times1000=1\,000\,000\,\text{m}^2$. Then $0.03\,\text{km}^2=0.03\times1\,000\,000=30\,000\,\text{m}^2$.

challenge_questions.statement: A rectangular tank has a base $2$ m by $1.5$ m and contains $2400$ litres of water. Find the depth of the water. A further $300$ litres are poured in; by how much does the depth rise?
challenge_questions.answer: Depth $=0.8$ m; the depth rises by a further $0.1$ m.
challenge_questions.full_solution: $2400\,\ell=2.4\,\text{m}^3$; base area $=2\times1.5=3\,\text{m}^2$, so depth $=2.4\div3=0.8$ m. Adding $300\,\ell=0.3\,\text{m}^3$ raises the depth by $0.3\div3=0.1$ m.

challenge_questions.statement: A leaking tap drips $0.05$ ml every second. How many litres are wasted in one day?
challenge_questions.full_solution: One day has $24\times60\times60=86\,400$ seconds. Total $=0.05\times86\,400=4320$ ml $=4.32$ litres.

challenge_questions.statement: A cube has a volume of exactly $8$ litres. Find its side length in cm and its total surface area in $\text{m}^2$.
challenge_questions.full_solution: $8$ litres $=8000\,\text{cm}^3$, so the side is $\sqrt[3]{8000}=20$ cm. Total surface area $=6\times20^2=2400\,\text{cm}^2$; converting: $2400\div10\,000=0.24\,\text{m}^2$.

challenge_questions.statement: A tank measuring $1.2$ m by $0.9$ m by $0.6$ m is full of water. Water is poured into $\tfrac14$-litre glasses. How many glasses can be filled?
challenge_questions.full_solution: Volume $=1.2\times0.9\times0.6=0.648\,\text{m}^3=648$ litres. Number of glasses $=648\div0.25=2592$.

mcq.stem: What is $2.5\,\text{m}^2$ converted to $\text{cm}^2$?

options.why_wrong: Uses the LENGTH conversion factor (100) instead of the area factor (10 000): the factor must be squared for an area conversion.
Uses the VOLUME conversion factor ($1\,000\,000$) instead of the area factor, cubing the length factor rather than squaring it.
Divides instead of multiplying: cm are SMALLER than m, so the number of cm$^2$ must be larger than the number of m$^2$, not smaller.

mcq.explanation: The area factor from m to cm is $100^2=10\,000$, so $2.5\times10\,000=25\,000\,\text{cm}^2$.

mcq.stem: What is $0.6\,\text{m}^3$ converted to litres?

options.why_wrong: Forgets to multiply by the $\text{m}^3$-to-litre factor of $1000$ altogether, leaving the number unchanged.
Uses the AREA factor ($10\,000$) instead of the correct volume–capacity factor of $1000$: $0.6\times10\,000=6000$.
Multiplies by $100$ (the m–cm LENGTH factor) instead of by $1000$, the $\text{m}^3$-to-litre factor: $0.6\times100=60$.

mcq.explanation: $1\,\text{m}^3=1000$ litres exactly, so $0.6\times1000=600$ litres.

mcq.stem: Which calculation correctly converts $3.4$ km to metres?

options.why_wrong: Divides when going to a SMALLER unit (m is smaller than km), which always needs MORE of the new unit, not fewer — so the operation must be multiplication.
Uses the wrong factor (100 is the m–cm factor, not the km–m factor), and divides instead of multiplying.
Multiplies by the correct TYPE of operation but uses $100$ (the m–cm factor) instead of $1000$ (the km–m factor).

mcq.explanation: Metres are smaller than kilometres, so convert by multiplying by the km-to-m factor, $1000$: $3.4\times1000=3400$ m.

mcq.stem: What is $1\,\text{cm}^3$ equal to, in millilitres?

options.why_wrong: Confuses the volume–capacity link with the cm–mm LENGTH factor ($10$); the link between $\text{cm}^3$ and ml is exactly $1$, not $10$.
Confuses $\text{cm}^3$ with litres: it is $1000\,\text{cm}^3$ that equals $1$ litre $=1000$ ml, not $1\,\text{cm}^3$.
Inverts the correct relationship, as if converting FROM ml TO $\text{cm}^3$ using the wrong direction.

mcq.explanation: $1\,\text{ml}=1\,\text{cm}^3$ exactly: this is the key fact linking the volume and capacity systems.

mcq.stem: A fish tank is a cuboid $60$ cm by $40$ cm by $20$ cm. What is its capacity in litres?

options.why_wrong: Forgets to divide the volume in $\text{cm}^3$ ($48\,000$) by $1000$ to reach litres, leaving an answer $1000$ times too large.
Divides by $100\,000$ instead of $1000$, as if using the area factor $10\,000$ combined with a further division by $10$.
Divides the volume in $\text{cm}^3$ by $100$ instead of $1000$, confusing the length factor with the volume–capacity factor.

mcq.explanation: Volume $=60\times40\times20=48\,000\,\text{cm}^3$; since $1\,\ell=1000\,\text{cm}^3$, this is $48\,000\div1000=48$ litres.

mcq.stem: Which operation correctly converts $450$ cm to metres?

options.why_wrong: Multiplies when going to a LARGER unit (m is larger than cm), which always needs FEWER of the new unit, not more — so the operation must be division.
Uses the wrong factor (10 is the cm–mm factor, not the cm–m factor), even though the direction (dividing) is correct.
Gets both the factor (10 instead of 100) and the direction wrong at once.

mcq.explanation: Metres are larger than centimetres, so convert by dividing by the cm-to-m factor, $100$.

flashcards.front: Metric length units, smallest to largest
flashcards.back: mm, cm, m, km — with $1\,\text{cm}=10\,\text{mm}$, $1\,\text{m}=100\,\text{cm}$, $1\,\text{km}=1000\,\text{m}$.

flashcards.front: Length factor $k$ → area factor? → volume factor?
flashcards.back: Area factor $=k^2$; volume factor $=k^3$.

flashcards.front: $1\,\text{m}^2$ in $\text{cm}^2$? $1\,\text{m}^3$ in $\text{cm}^3$?
Link between volume and capacity
Going to a smaller unit vs. a larger unit
flashcards.back: Smaller unit → MORE of them needed → multiply. Larger unit → FEWER needed → divide.

flashcards.front: True or false: $1\,\text{m}^2=100\,\text{cm}^2$.
flashcards.back: False. $100$ is the LENGTH factor; for area it must be squared, giving $1\,\text{m}^2=10\,000\,\text{cm}^2$.

flashcards.front: True or false: a rectangle $2$ m by $50$ cm has area $2\times50=100$.
flashcards.back: False. The two lengths are in different units; convert first (e.g. to cm): $200\times50=10\,000\,\text{cm}^2$ ($=1\,\text{m}^2$).

flashcards.front: Area factor vs. volume factor for the same length factor $k$
flashcards.back: Area uses $k^2$; volume uses $k^3$ — always one extra power of $k$ for volume than for area.

flashcards.front: Mass units
flashcards.back: $1\,\text{kg}=1000\,\text{g}$; $1\,\text{tonne}=1000\,\text{kg}$.

flashcards.front: Rectangle given in two different units — first step?
flashcards.back: Convert BOTH lengths to the same unit before multiplying to find the area.

flashcards.front: Why does an area conversion square the length factor?
flashcards.back: Area counts unit SQUARES in two directions at once, so each of the two dimensions contributes one factor of $k$: $k\times k=k^2$.

flashcards.front: A cuboid's volume is known in $\text{cm}^3$. How do you find its capacity in litres?
flashcards.back: Divide the volume in $\text{cm}^3$ by $1000$.

flashcards.front: A cube of side $10$ cm holds how much?
flashcards.back: Exactly $1$ litre, since $10\times10\times10=1000\,\text{cm}^3=1\,\ell$.

flashcards.front: Quick sense checks for typical sizes
flashcards.back: A door is about $2$ m high; a cup holds about $250$ ml; a can of drink has a mass of about $350$ g.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Applying the length conversion factor directly when converting an area or a volume, e.g. writing $1\,\text{m}^2=100\,\text{cm}^2$ or $1\,\text{m}^3=100\,\text{cm}^3$.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The length factor (100, for m↔cm) is the one students memorise first and most confidently, so under time pressure it gets reused for every unit conversion regardless of whether the quantity is a length, an area or a volume.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner's converted area or volume is far too small compared with a quick sketch or sense-check (e.g. claiming a 1 m² tile is only 100 cm², about the size of a postcard).
misconceptions.correct_model: A length factor $k$ becomes $k^2$ for an area conversion and $k^3$ for a volume conversion, because area counts squares and volume counts cubes. For m↔cm, $k=100$, so area uses $100^2=10\,000$ and volume uses $100^3=1\,000\,000$.
misconceptions.remediation: Before converting, write the LENGTH factor first (e.g. 100 for m↔cm), then explicitly square it for an area question or cube it for a volume question — never skip straight to the final factor from memory.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Using the AREA factor (e.g. 10 000 for m↔cm) when the question is really about volume, or the volume factor when the question is about area — the two squared/cubed factors get swapped or confused with each other.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Once a student has learned that area conversions need 'the length factor squared', the extra step of also cubing it for volume is easy to forget or misapply, especially when area and volume questions appear side by side in the same exercise set.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner writes $1\,\text{m}^3=10\,000\,\text{cm}^3$ (the AREA factor) instead of $1\,000\,000\,\text{cm}^3$, or the reverse error for an area question.
misconceptions.correct_model: Always ask first: 'is this a length ($k$), an area ($k^2$) or a volume ($k^3$) conversion?' before picking a numerical factor — the three factors for m↔cm are 100, 10 000 and 1 000 000 respectively, and none of them can substitute for another.
misconceptions.remediation: Build all three factors from the same length factor every time, in order, rather than recalling the area/volume factor from memory in isolation: $k=100\Rightarrow k^2=10\,000\Rightarrow k^3=1\,000\,000$.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Assuming every conversion from a named unit to another always means MULTIPLYING, regardless of whether the new unit is smaller or larger (or the reverse: always dividing).
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Early practice often converts from a larger unit to a smaller one (km to m, m to cm), where multiplying is always correct, so the direction check gets skipped and 'multiply' becomes an automatic habit that then fails on the first small-to-large conversion.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner multiplies when converting 450 cm to m (giving an absurdly large answer) or divides when converting 3.4 km to m (giving an absurdly small one).
misconceptions.correct_model: Decide the direction FIRST: going to a smaller unit needs MORE of them, so multiply; going to a larger unit needs FEWER, so divide. Ask 'should my number get bigger or smaller?' before doing any arithmetic.
misconceptions.remediation: Before calculating, write down in words which unit is bigger, then state out loud whether the answer should be a bigger or a smaller number than the one given — only then perform the multiplication or division.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Calculating an area or a volume directly from lengths given in two DIFFERENT units, without converting them to a common unit first — e.g. treating a rectangle 2 m by 50 cm as having area $2\times50=100$.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The multiplication step $(\text{length})\times(\text{width})$ feels complete once two numbers are substituted into the formula, so the separate check 'are these two numbers in the same unit?' is easy to skip, especially when a problem states lengths in mixed units deliberately.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner's area or volume answer has no sensible unit attached, or is wildly inconsistent with a quick estimate (e.g. a rectangle described as roughly 2 m by half a metre coming out as '100', with no stated unit that makes sense).
misconceptions.correct_model: Convert every length in the problem to the SAME unit before substituting into any area or volume formula: the rectangle 2 m by 50 cm is $200\,\text{cm}\times50\,\text{cm}=10\,000\,\text{cm}^2$, or equivalently $2\,\text{m}\times0.5\,\text{m}=1\,\text{m}^2$.
misconceptions.remediation: Make 'same units?' the first written check on every area/volume question, before writing down the formula — circle every unit given in the question and convert any that don't match the others.

common_mistakes.mistake: Calculating an area or volume from lengths given in two different units without converting first.
common_mistakes.why: The multiplication $(\text{length})\times(\text{width})$ feels complete as soon as two numbers are substituted, so the separate check 'are these the same unit?' is easy to skip.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Circle every unit in the question first, and convert any that don't match before writing down the formula.

common_mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to state the unit in the final answer.
common_mistakes.why: After a long calculation, the final number itself feels like 'the answer', and the unit gets treated as an afterthought.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Write the unit next to the formula BEFORE substituting numbers, so it is never left off the final line.

common_mistakes.mistake: Rounding a metric conversion to 3 significant figures when it should be given exactly.
common_mistakes.why: Most IGCSE calculator-paper answers are rounded to 3 s.f. by habit, but metric conversions (km–m, m–cm, L–ml, …) are exact multiplications or divisions by a power of 10.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Give the exact value for a pure unit conversion; round to 3 s.f. only once a further (non-exact) calculation, such as a square root or division by $\pi$, has been performed.

exam_notes: Metric conversions are NOT printed in the List of formulas: you must know them from memory, including that an area factor is squared and a volume factor is cubed.
Conversions between metric units are normally exact: give the exact value rather than rounding to 3 significant figures, unless the question tells you otherwise.
Always write the unit with your final answer — a correct number with the wrong or a missing unit can lose the final mark.

When a question mixes units in the given information (e.g. a wall in metres with a window in centimetres), convert everything to one unit first and show this conversion as your first line of working, to secure early method marks even if a later step goes wrong.

summary.big_idea: A length conversion multiplies by a scale factor $k$; an area conversion multiplies by $k^2$ and a volume conversion by $k^3$ — because area counts squares and volume counts cubes of the same unit.
key_points: Length: $1\,\text{km}=1000\,\text{m}$, $1\,\text{m}=100\,\text{cm}$, $1\,\text{cm}=10\,\text{mm}$. Mass: $1\,\text{kg}=1000\,\text{g}$. Capacity: $1\,\ell=1000\,\text{ml}$.
Area factors are the length factor SQUARED; volume factors are the length factor CUBED — never use the length factor unchanged for an area or volume.
Volume and capacity are linked exactly: $1\,\text{ml}=1\,\text{cm}^3$, $1\,\ell=1000\,\text{cm}^3$, $1\,\text{m}^3=1000\,\ell$.
Decide the DIRECTION first: smaller target unit → multiply; larger target unit → divide.
Convert every length in a problem to the SAME unit before calculating an area or a volume, and state the unit in the final answer.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Find the LENGTH conversion factor first, then square it for an area question or cube it for a volume question — and always convert every length to the same unit before calculating.

02_Area_and_Perimeter.json.title: Area and Perimeter
02_Area_and_Perimeter.json.subject: Mathematics
02_Area_and_Perimeter.json.course_label: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 · Mensuration · Core + Extended

objectives.statement: Find the perimeter and area of a rectangle and a square.
Find the area of a triangle using $A=\tfrac12bh$, correctly identifying the perpendicular height, including when it falls outside an obtuse triangle.
Find the area and perimeter of a parallelogram and a trapezium, using the correct perpendicular height rather than a slanted side.
Use an area or perimeter formula 'backwards' to find a missing base, height or parallel side, including when a side is given as an algebraic expression.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise a right angle and identify when two line segments are perpendicular to each other.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every area formula in this lesson (triangle, parallelogram, trapezium) needs the PERPENDICULAR height, not a slanted side; without being able to spot a right angle in a diagram, the wrong length gets substituted every time.

prerequisites.statement: Solve a simple linear equation in one unknown, such as $2(2w+w)=30$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every 'working backwards' problem in this lesson (missing width, missing height, missing parallel side, algebraic sides) ends in exactly this kind of one-step or two-step equation.

prerequisites.statement: Multiply and divide decimals, and substitute a number into a simple algebraic expression such as $2x+1$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Both the numerical substitutions (e.g. $A=\tfrac12\times9\times6$) and the algebraic-side problems in this lesson depend on comfortable substitution and arithmetic with decimals.

prerequisites.statement: Convert between units of length, such as between metres and centimetres (Lesson 5.1).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A handful of context problems in this lesson (fencing a lawn, painting a wall) only make sense once every length is already expressed in a single, consistent unit.

diagnostic_items.question: Why is the area of a triangle $\tfrac12bh$ and not $bh$?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: A triangle is exactly HALF of a parallelogram (or rectangle) built on the same base and the same perpendicular height, so its area is half of $bh$.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Because that's the formula you're given to memorise.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Recites the formula without connecting it to why it is true, which leaves no way to rebuild it if forgotten under exam pressure.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks whether the learner can justify the formula from the rectangle/parallelogram link (the related idea), not just recall it.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Sketch a parallelogram with a diagonal drawn in, splitting it into two congruent triangles; show that each triangle's area must be exactly half of the parallelogram's $bh$.

diagnostic_items.question: Can the height of a triangle be longer than the two sides that meet at its top vertex? Can it lie outside the triangle?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: No, the height can never be longer than either of those two sides (it is the shortest, PERPENDICULAR distance from the vertex to the base line, equal to one of the sides only in a right-angled triangle). Yes, it can lie outside the triangle, when the angle at one end of the base is obtuse.

common_wrong_answers.answer: No, the height always has to be drawn inside the triangle.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Has only seen acute or right-angled triangles, so has not yet met the case where the perpendicular foot falls beyond the base and the base line must be extended.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks whether the learner's mental model of 'height' already includes the obtuse-triangle case, before it appears unexpectedly in an exercise.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Draw an obtuse triangle and physically extend the base line with a dashed segment to show the perpendicular foot landing outside the original base.

diagnostic_items.question: A parallelogram has sides $10$ cm and $6$ cm. Is its area $60\,\text{cm}^2$? Explain.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Not necessarily. $60\,\text{cm}^2$ would only be correct if $6$ cm were the PERPENDICULAR height to the $10$ cm base; since a parallelogram (unless it is a rectangle) leans over, its true perpendicular height to that base is LESS than $6$ cm, so the real area is smaller than $60\,\text{cm}^2$.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Yes, because area is always the two given sides multiplied together.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Over-generalises the rectangle rule $A=lw$ to every four-sided shape, without checking whether the second side given is actually the perpendicular height.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Tests the central misconception of this lesson directly: that any two side lengths of a parallelogram can be multiplied to get the area.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Sketch a visibly 'leaning' parallelogram with sides 10 and 6 and mark the true (shorter) perpendicular height with a right-angle symbol, to make the gap between the slant side and the height visible.

diagnostic_items.question: Which of the formulas for the area of a rectangle, triangle, parallelogram and trapezium are printed in the exam's List of formulas?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Only the triangle, $A=\tfrac12bh$. The rectangle, parallelogram and trapezium formulas must be memorised.

common_wrong_answers.answer: All four, since they're all 'basic' shapes.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Assumes that because a formula is simple, it must be provided, rather than checking the actual exam formula sheet.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks a genuine exam-technique fact that affects revision priorities, not just mathematical understanding.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Look up the real List of formulas (front of the exam paper) and highlight exactly which mensuration formulas are present, to build an accurate memorise/given list.

theory_blocks.title: Every formula comes from the rectangle
theory_blocks.body: Every formula in this lesson comes from [[blue:the rectangle]]. A parallelogram can be cut and moved to make a rectangle of the same base and height; a triangle is exactly half of a rectangle or parallelogram with the same base and height; a trapezium is exactly half of a parallelogram made from two copies of itself. If a formula is ever forgotten, it can always be rebuilt from this one picture.

theory_blocks.title: Rectangles and squares
theory_blocks.body:
Rectangle with length $l$ and width $w$:
$$P=2(l+w),\qquad A=lw.$$
Square of side $a$: $P=4a$ and $A=a^2$. None of these formulas is given in the exam.

theory_blocks.title: The triangle: base and perpendicular height
theory_blocks.body:
Any side of a triangle can be chosen as the **base**. The **height** is the PERPENDICULAR distance from that base to the opposite vertex — it is not a slanted side, unless the triangle happens to be right-angled.
$$A=\tfrac12\,bh\qquad\text{(given in the List of formulas)}.$$
The perimeter is simply the sum of the three sides. In an obtuse triangle, the perpendicular foot can fall OUTSIDE the triangle; the base line is then extended with a dashed line, but the formula is unchanged.

assets.caption: In the obtuse triangle $ABC$ the base $b=AB$ has to be extended (green dashed) before the perpendicular height $h$ from $C$ can be drawn; the height falls outside the triangle, but $A=\tfrac12bh$ still applies.
assets.purpose: Show that the perpendicular height of an obtuse triangle can fall outside the triangle, on an extension of the base.

theory_blocks.title: Three common triangle errors
theory_blocks.body:
- [[red:Forgetting the $\tfrac12$]]: $b\times h$ is the area of the RECTANGLE (or parallelogram) with that base and height, not of the triangle.
- Using a slanted side as the height. In a triangle with sides $13,13,10$, the height onto the base $10$ is $12$, not $13$.
- Mixing up units: the perimeter is in cm, the area in $\text{cm}^2$.

theory_blocks.title: The parallelogram
theory_blocks.body:
A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides. Cutting off a triangle from one end and sliding it to the other end turns it into a rectangle with the SAME base and the same perpendicular height, which is why:
$$A=bh,\qquad P=2(b+s),$$
where $b$ is the base, $h$ the perpendicular height, and $s$ the length of the slanted side. The area formula is not given in the exam.

assets.caption: Cutting the shaded triangle off the left-hand end of the parallelogram and sliding it to the right-hand end makes a rectangle with the same base $b$ and the same perpendicular height $h$, so the two areas are equal.
assets.purpose: Make the cut-and-slide argument behind $A=bh$ for a parallelogram visible.

theory_blocks.title: The slant side is not the height
theory_blocks.body: In a parallelogram with base $8.5$ cm, slant side $5$ cm and perpendicular height $4$ cm, the area is $8.5\times4=34\,\text{cm}^2$ — NOT $8.5\times5$. The slant side is only needed for the perimeter.

theory_blocks.title: The trapezium
theory_blocks.body:
A trapezium has exactly one pair of parallel sides, $a$ and $b$; the perpendicular distance between them is the height $h$. Taking two identical trapezia and turning one around forms a parallelogram of base $a+b$ and height $h$, so one trapezium is exactly half of it:
$$A=\tfrac12(a+b)\,h.$$
The perimeter is the sum of all four sides. The area formula is not given in the exam.

assets.caption: Left: a trapezium with parallel sides $a$ and $b$ and perpendicular height $h$. Right: a second copy turned round fits onto the first to make a parallelogram of base $a+b$ and height $h$, so one trapezium is half of it.
assets.purpose: Label $a$, $b$ and $h$ on a trapezium and show the two-copies construction that gives $A=\tfrac12(a+b)h$.

theory_blocks.title: The trapezium area is an average × height
theory_blocks.body: $\tfrac12(a+b)$ is the AVERAGE of the two parallel sides. So a trapezium's area is (average parallel side) $\times$ (height) — exactly like a rectangle whose width is that average, which is why its area must lie strictly between the two rectangles $a\times h$ and $b\times h$.

theory_blocks.title: A sense check for trapezium area
theory_blocks.body: A trapezium's area must always lie between the areas of the two rectangles $a\times h$ and $b\times h$ built on its shorter and longer parallel sides. For parallel sides $9$ and $15$ with height $7$: $9\times7=63<84<105=15\times7$ — a quick way to catch an answer that is clearly too big or too small.

theory_blocks.title: A method for every shape in this lesson
theory_blocks.body:
1. Draw (or redraw) the shape and label every known length; mark the perpendicular height with a right-angle sign.
2. Write the formula, then substitute, keeping every length in the SAME unit.
3. For a missing side: write 'formula $=$ known area (or perimeter)' and solve the resulting equation.
4. State the units: cm for a perimeter, $\text{cm}^2$ for an area.

keywords.definition: The total distance around the edge of a shape, measured in a length unit such as cm.
The amount of flat surface a shape covers, measured in a square unit such as $\text{cm}^2$.
A chosen side of a triangle, parallelogram or trapezium, used together with the perpendicular height to find the area.
The shortest distance from a base to the opposite vertex or side, meeting the base at a right angle.
A quadrilateral with two pairs of parallel sides.
A quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides.
A side of a parallelogram or trapezium that is not perpendicular to the base, and so cannot be used as the height.
A triangle with one angle greater than $90^{\circ}$; its perpendicular height can fall outside the triangle.

worked_examples.statement: Rectangle. A rectangle measures $12.5$ cm by $8$ cm. Find its perimeter and area.
worked_examples.interpretation: Substituting directly into the two memorised rectangle formulas, with no working-backwards step, establishes the baseline method before anything harder is attempted.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Writing the area with the perimeter's unit (cm) instead of $\text{cm}^2$, or vice versa.

worked_examples.statement: Working backwards. The perimeter of a rectangle is $30$ cm and its length is twice its width. Find its area.
reasoning: Let the width be $w$, so the length is $2w$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Writing every side in terms of ONE letter before forming the perimeter equation is the general method for every 'working backwards' problem in this lesson, whatever shape is involved.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Solving for $w$ and stopping there, forgetting that the question asked for the AREA, not the width.

worked_examples.statement: Triangles. (a) Find the area of a triangle with base $9$ cm and height $6$ cm. (b) An obtuse triangle has a side $10$ cm long, and the perpendicular distance from the opposite vertex to the LINE of that side is $4$ cm. Find its area. (c) A triangle has area $12\,\text{cm}^2$ and base $8$ cm. Find its height.
reasoning: (b) Use the $10$ cm side as the base: $A=\tfrac12\times10\times4=20$; the other two sides are not needed at all.
worked_examples.interpretation: Part (b) shows that an obtuse triangle's area needs only the chosen base and its perpendicular height — the other two side lengths given in a diagram are often irrelevant distractors.
worked_examples.common_mistake: In part (c), computing $12\div8=1.5$ and stopping, forgetting the formula is $\tfrac12bh$, not $bh$, so the $\tfrac12$ must also be undone.

worked_examples.statement: Parallelogram and trapezium. (a) A parallelogram has base $8.5$ cm, slanted side $5$ cm and perpendicular height $4$ cm. Find its area and perimeter. (b) A trapezium has parallel sides $7$ cm and $13$ cm; the perpendicular side is $8$ cm and the slanted side is $10$ cm. Find its area and perimeter.
reasoning: (b) The height is the PERPENDICULAR side, $h=8$ cm (the slanted $10$ cm is not the height). $A=\tfrac12(7+13)\times8=\tfrac12\times20\times8=80$; $P=7+13+8+10=38$.
worked_examples.interpretation: In both parts, the area uses only the perpendicular height, while the perimeter needs EVERY side including the slanted ones — the two calculations draw on almost entirely different given numbers.
worked_examples.common_mistake: In part (a), using the slant side $5$ in the area ($8.5\times5$) instead of the height $4$ — see the related idea.

worked_examples.statement: Finding a missing height. A trapezium has area $84\,\text{cm}^2$ and parallel sides $9$ cm and $15$ cm. Find the distance between the parallel sides.
worked_examples.interpretation: Writing 'formula $=$ known area' and solving for the one unknown number is exactly the method of the related idea, applied here to the trapezium's height instead of a rectangle's width.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Writing $84=\tfrac12(9+15)h$ but then forgetting to halve $(9+15)$ before dividing, using $24h=84$ instead of $12h=84$.

worked_examples.statement: Algebraic sides. A rectangle has length $(2x+1)$ cm and width $(x+1)$ cm. Its perimeter is $34$ cm. Find $x$ and the area.
worked_examples.interpretation: An algebraic side is just a side written with an unknown instead of a number; the same perimeter formula and the same method (form an equation, solve, then substitute back for the area) still apply unchanged.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Stopping once $x=5$ is found, without substituting it back to find the actual length and width needed to calculate the area.

worked_examples.statement: In context. A rectangular wall $4.8$ m by $2.5$ m is to be painted. One litre of paint covers $6\,\text{m}^2$. How many litres are needed?
worked_examples.interpretation: A real-world 'how much paint/material' question is almost always an ordinary area calculation in disguise, followed by one division by a coverage rate.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Dividing $6\div12$ instead of $12\div6$, inverting the rate and giving an answer less than one when more than one litre is clearly needed.

guided_exercises.statement: A rectangle has perimeter $22$ cm. Its length is $3$ cm more than its width. Find its area.
hints: Let the width be $w$; write the length in terms of $w$ too.
Form an equation from the perimeter formula $P=2(l+w)$, and solve it for $w$ before finding the area.
guided_exercises.full_solution: Let the width be $w$, so the length is $w+3$. Then $2\big[(w+3)+w\big]=22\Rightarrow2(2w+3)=22\Rightarrow2w+3=11\Rightarrow w=4$. So width $=4$ cm, length $=7$ cm, and $A=4\times7=28\,\text{cm}^2$.
common_errors: Writing the length as $3w$ instead of $w+3$, misreading '3 cm more than' as '3 times as much as'.

guided_exercises.statement: An isosceles triangle has two equal sides of $15$ cm and a base of $18$ cm. The perpendicular height from the apex to the base splits the triangle into two congruent right-angled triangles. Find the triangle's area.
hints: The height splits the base exactly in half, so one right-angled triangle has a known hypotenuse ($15$) and a known shorter leg (half of $18$).
Use Pythagoras' theorem to find the height, then use the full base ($18$, not the half) in the area formula.
guided_exercises.full_solution: Half the base is $9$ cm. By Pythagoras, $h^2=15^2-9^2=225-81=144$, so $h=12$ cm. Area $=\tfrac12\times18\times12=108\,\text{cm}^2$.
common_errors: Using the HALF base ($9$) in the final area formula instead of the full base ($18$), after correctly using the half base to find the height.

guided_exercises.statement: A trapezium has area $45\,\text{cm}^2$ and height $6$ cm. Its parallel sides are $x$ cm and $(x+4)$ cm. Find $x$ and state the lengths of the two parallel sides.
hints: Substitute the two parallel sides and the height into the trapezium area formula, and set the result equal to $45$.
Simplify $\tfrac12\big[x+(x+4)\big]\times6$ before solving the equation for $x$.
guided_exercises.answer: $x=5.5$; the parallel sides are $5.5$ cm and $9.5$ cm.
guided_exercises.full_solution: $45=\tfrac12\big[x+(x+4)\big]\times6=3(2x+4)=6x+12$. So $6x=33$ and $x=5.5$. The parallel sides are $5.5$ cm and $9.5$ cm. Check: $\tfrac12(5.5+9.5)\times6=\tfrac12\times15\times6=45$. ✓
common_errors: Forgetting to multiply by the height $6$ at all, solving $\tfrac12\big[x+(x+4)\big]=45$ instead of the full area equation.

exercises.statement: A rectangle is $14$ cm by $6.5$ cm. Find its perimeter and area.
common_errors: Giving the area in cm instead of $\text{cm}^2$, or the perimeter in $\text{cm}^2$.

exercises.statement: A square has perimeter $36$ cm. Find its side and its area.
common_errors: Dividing by $2$ instead of $4$, confusing a square's perimeter formula with a rectangle's.

exercises.statement: Find the area of a triangle with base $12$ cm and height $7.5$ cm.
exercises.full_solution: $A=\tfrac12\times12\times7.5=45\,\text{cm}^2$.
common_errors: Omitting the $\tfrac12$, giving $90$ instead of $45$.

exercises.statement: A triangle has area $30\,\text{cm}^2$ and base $12$ cm. Find its height.
exercises.full_solution: $30=\tfrac12\times12\times h=6h$, so $h=30\div6=5$.
common_errors: Dividing $30$ by $12$ directly, giving $2.5$ and forgetting to account for the $\tfrac12$ in the formula.

exercises.statement: Find the area of a parallelogram with base $9.5$ cm and perpendicular height $6$ cm.
exercises.full_solution: $A=bh=9.5\times6=57\,\text{cm}^2$.
common_errors: Multiplying by $\tfrac12$, confusing the parallelogram formula with the triangle formula.

exercises.statement: A parallelogram has sides $10$ cm and $7$ cm. The perpendicular height to the $10$ cm side is $5.6$ cm. Find (a) its area; (b) the perpendicular height to the $7$ cm side.
exercises.full_solution: (a) $A=10\times5.6=56\,\text{cm}^2$. (b) The AREA is the same whichever side is used as the base, so $56=7\times h\Rightarrow h=56\div7=8$ cm.
common_errors: In (b), assuming the height to the $7$ cm side must also be $5.6$, instead of recalculating from the fixed, already-known area.

exercises.statement: Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides $8$ cm and $12$ cm which are $6.5$ cm apart.
exercises.full_solution: $A=\tfrac12(8+12)\times6.5=\tfrac12\times20\times6.5=65\,\text{cm}^2$.
common_errors: Forgetting to add the two parallel sides before halving, using $8+12\times6.5$ with the wrong order of operations.

exercises.statement: A trapezium has parallel sides $5$ cm and $11$ cm, a perpendicular side of $8$ cm and a slanted side of $10$ cm. Find its perimeter and area.
exercises.full_solution: $P=5+11+8+10=34$ cm. $A=\tfrac12(5+11)\times8=64\,\text{cm}^2$ (using the PERPENDICULAR side, $8$, as the height; the slanted $10$ cm side is not needed for the area).
common_errors: Using the slanted side ($10$) as the height in the area formula instead of the perpendicular side ($8$).

exercises.statement: A rectangular lawn is $18$ m by $12.5$ m. (a) Fencing costs \$4.50 per metre. Find the cost of fencing all round. (b) Grass seed is sold at $1$ kg per $25\,\text{m}^2$. How many kilograms are needed for the whole lawn?
common_errors: Using the AREA instead of the PERIMETER when costing the fencing in part (a), since both numbers appear in the same question.

exercises.statement: A rectangle has perimeter $42$ cm and its length is twice its width. Find its area.
exercises.full_solution: Let the width be $w$: $2(2w+w)=42\Rightarrow6w=42\Rightarrow w=7$, $l=14$, $A=14\times7=98\,\text{cm}^2$.
common_errors: Finding $w=7$ correctly but stopping there instead of continuing to the area.

exercises.statement: A trapezium has area $90\,\text{cm}^2$ and parallel sides $8$ cm and $12$ cm. Find the distance between the parallel sides.
exercises.full_solution: $90=\tfrac12(8+12)h=10h\Rightarrow h=9$.
common_errors: Using $8+12=20$ as the divisor directly without halving it first, giving $h=4.5$ instead of $9$.

exercises.statement: A rectangle has length $(3x+1)$ cm and width $(x+2)$ cm. Its perimeter is $38$ cm. Find $x$ and the area.
exercises.full_solution: $2(4x+3)=38\Rightarrow4x+3=19\Rightarrow x=4$; length $13$, width $6$; $A=13\times6=78\,\text{cm}^2$.
common_errors: Solving correctly for $x$ but then using $x$ itself (instead of the resulting length and width) in the area calculation.

exercises.statement: Triangle $ABC$ has vertices $A(1,1)$, $B(7,1)$ and $C(4,6)$. Find its area.
exercises.full_solution: $AB$ lies along $y=1$ and has length $6$ (a convenient horizontal base); the perpendicular height from $C$ to this line is $6-1=5$. $A=\tfrac12\times6\times5=15$.
common_errors: Not noticing that $AB$ is horizontal, and attempting a longer, more error-prone method for the base or height instead.

exercises.statement: A trapezium has parallel sides $x$ cm and $(x+6)$ cm, and height $4$ cm. Its area is $56\,\text{cm}^2$. Find $x$.
exercises.full_solution: $\tfrac12(2x+6)\times4=56\Rightarrow4x+12=56\Rightarrow4x=44\Rightarrow x=11$.
common_errors: Forgetting the $\times4$ and solving $\tfrac12(2x+6)=56$, i.e. $x+3=56$, giving $x=53$ instead of $11$.

exercises.statement: An isosceles trapezium has parallel sides $6$ cm and $14$ cm and slanted sides $5$ cm. Find its height and area.
exercises.full_solution: Each end sticks out $(14-6)\div2=4$ cm. By Pythagoras, $h^2=5^2-4^2=9$, so $h=3$ cm. $A=\tfrac12(6+14)\times3=30\,\text{cm}^2$.
common_errors: Using the slanted side ($5$) directly as the height instead of using Pythagoras to find the true perpendicular height — see the related idea.

exercises.statement: A parallelogram has area $48\,\text{cm}^2$ and base $12$ cm. A triangle has the same base and the same perpendicular height. Find the area of the triangle.
exercises.full_solution: Height of the parallelogram $=48\div12=4$ cm. The triangle's area is HALF of a parallelogram with the same base and height: $\tfrac12\times12\times4=24\,\text{cm}^2$.
common_errors: Forgetting the $\tfrac12$ and giving the triangle's area as $48\,\text{cm}^2$, the same as the parallelogram's.

exercises.statement: The diagram shows triangle $PQR$, which is obtuse at $Q$. $QR=15$ cm, $PQ=10$ cm, and the perpendicular distance from $P$ to the line $QR$ is $8$ cm. Find the area of the triangle.
exercises.full_solution: Take $QR$ as the base: $b=15$ cm and the perpendicular height to that base is $h=8$ cm (it meets the line $QR$ outside the triangle, which does not matter). $A=\tfrac12\times15\times8=60\,\text{cm}^2$. The length $PQ=10$ cm is not needed.
common_errors: Using the slanted side $PQ=10$ cm as the height and getting $\tfrac12\times15\times10=75\,\text{cm}^2$.
Thinking the formula fails because the foot of the height lies outside the triangle.

assets.caption: Triangle $PQR$ with $QR=15$ cm and $PQ=10$ cm; the perpendicular height of $8$ cm from $P$ meets the line $QR$ outside the triangle.
assets.purpose: Give the lesson one exercise that has to be read from a diagram, with a slanted side as a distractor.

exam_questions.statement:
A rectangle has length $(3x-2)$ cm and width $(x+4)$ cm. Its perimeter is $44$ cm.
(a) Form an equation in $x$ and solve it. [3]
(b) Find the area of the rectangle. [2]
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) $2\big[(3x-2)+(x+4)\big]=44\Rightarrow2(4x+2)=44\Rightarrow4x+2=22\Rightarrow4x=20\Rightarrow x=5$. (b) Length $=3(5)-2=13$ cm, width $=5+4=9$ cm; $A=13\times9=117\,\text{cm}^2$.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for a correct perimeter expression $2\big[(3x-2)+(x+4)\big]=44$; M1 for simplifying to $4x+2=22$ (or equivalent); A1 for $x=5$
(b) M1 for substituting $x=5$ to find both the length ($13$) and the width ($9$); A1 for $117\,\text{cm}^2$ (follow through on their $x$).
common_errors: Finding $x=5$ correctly in (a) but then substituting $x=5$ directly into the perimeter formula again in (b) instead of into the length and width, and reporting $44$ (or half of it) as if it were the area.

exam_questions.statement:
A trapezium has parallel sides $11$ cm and $19$ cm and area $112.5\,\text{cm}^2$.
(a) Calculate the height of the trapezium. [2]
(b) The trapezium's two slanted sides are each $8.5$ cm. Calculate its perimeter. [2]
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for $112.5=\tfrac12(11+19)h$ or equivalent; A1 for $h=7.5$
(b) M1 for adding all four sides; A1 for $47$ cm.
common_errors: In (b), using the height from (a) as if it were one of the sides needed for the perimeter, instead of the given slanted sides.

exam_questions.statement:
A triangle has sides $AB=10$ cm, $AC=10$ cm and $BC=16$ cm.
(a) Show that the perpendicular height from $A$ to $BC$ is $6$ cm. [3]
(b) Hence calculate the area of the triangle. [2]
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) The height from the apex of an isosceles triangle meets the base at its midpoint, so it splits $BC=16$ into two lengths of $8$. By Pythagoras, $h^2=10^2-8^2=100-64=36$, so $h=\sqrt{36}=6$ cm, as required. (b) $A=\tfrac12\times16\times6=48\,\text{cm}^2$.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for halving the base to get $8$; M1 for the correct Pythagoras statement $h^2=10^2-8^2$; A1 for showing $h=6$ with the concluding statement written (a bare $h^2=36$ with no final 'so $h=6$' line does not earn this mark on a 'show that' question)
(b) M1 for $\tfrac12\times16\times6$; A1 for $48\,\text{cm}^2$ (follow through on the given height $6$ even if (a) was not fully correct).
common_errors: Using the full base $16$ instead of the half-base $8$ in the Pythagoras step, producing a height that does not match the value the question asks you to show.

challenge_questions.statement: Explain, with a sketch, why the area of a parallelogram of base $b$ and perpendicular height $h$ equals $bh$, and why two triangles with the same base on the same parallel lines have equal areas.
challenge_questions.answer: Cutting a right-angled triangle from one slanted end of the parallelogram and attaching it at the other end produces a rectangle $b\times h$ of the same area; any two triangles sharing a base and lying between the same pair of parallel lines share the same base $b$ and the same perpendicular height $h$, so $\tfrac12bh$ is identical for both.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Cut a right-angled triangle from one slanted end of the parallelogram and slide it to the other end: a rectangle $b\times h$ results, with exactly the same area as the original parallelogram (nothing was added or removed, only moved). For the second part, two triangles with the same base $b$, both lying between the same pair of parallel lines, must have the same perpendicular distance $h$ between those lines, so $\tfrac12bh$ gives the same value for each.

challenge_questions.statement: A rectangle has perimeter $28$ cm and area $48\,\text{cm}^2$. By forming and solving an equation, find its dimensions.
challenge_questions.full_solution: $l+w=14$, so $w=14-l$; substituting into $lw=48$ gives $l(14-l)=48$, i.e. $l^2-14l+48=0$, which factorises as $(l-6)(l-8)=0$. So the dimensions are $6$ cm and $8$ cm.

challenge_questions.statement: A triangle has sides $13$ cm, $13$ cm and $10$ cm. Given that its height on the $10$ cm side is $12$ cm, find its area and the perpendicular height on one of the $13$ cm sides, correct to $3$ significant figures.
challenge_questions.answer: $A=60\,\text{cm}^2$; height on a $13$ cm side $\approx9.23$ cm.
challenge_questions.full_solution: $A=\tfrac12\times10\times12=60\,\text{cm}^2$. The AREA is the same whichever side is used as base, so using a $13$ cm side: $\tfrac12\times13\times h=60\Rightarrow h=120\div13=9.2307\ldots\approx9.23$ cm (3 s.f.).

challenge_questions.statement: Every side of a square is increased by $20\%$. Show that its area increases by $44\%$.
challenge_questions.answer: New area $=1.44a^2$, an increase of $44\%$, as required.
challenge_questions.full_solution: The new side is $1.2a$, so the new area is $(1.2a)^2=1.44a^2$, which is $44\%$ larger than the original area $a^2$, as required.

challenge_questions.statement: A rectangle is $5$ cm by $12$ cm, so its diagonal is $13$ cm. Find the perpendicular distance from a vertex not on the diagonal to the diagonal, correct to $3$ significant figures.
challenge_questions.full_solution: The diagonal splits the rectangle into two triangles, each of area $\tfrac12\times5\times12=30\,\text{cm}^2$. Using the diagonal ($13$) as the base of one such triangle: $\tfrac12\times13\times h=30\Rightarrow h=60\div13=4.6153\ldots\approx4.62$ cm (3 s.f.).

mcq.stem: A triangle has base $10$ cm and perpendicular height $6$ cm. What is its area?

options.why_wrong: Forgets the $\tfrac12$ in the triangle area formula, giving the area of a RECTANGLE with that base and height instead.
Adds the base and height ($10+6$) instead of multiplying them — confuses the area operation with a perimeter-style sum.
Halves BOTH the base and the height before multiplying ($5\times3=15$), which applies the $\tfrac12$ twice instead of once.

mcq.explanation: $A=\tfrac12bh=\tfrac12\times10\times6=30\,\text{cm}^2$.

mcq.stem: A parallelogram has base $9$ cm, a slanted side of $7$ cm, and perpendicular height $5$ cm. What is its area?

options.why_wrong: Uses the SLANTED side ($7$) in place of the perpendicular height ($5$); the slanted side is only needed for the perimeter.
Computes $2(9+7)$, the PERIMETER formula, instead of an area — confuses the two calculations entirely.
Uses the TRIANGLE formula $\tfrac12bh$ instead of the parallelogram formula $bh$.

mcq.explanation: A parallelogram's area is base $\times$ perpendicular height: $9\times5=45\,\text{cm}^2$.

mcq.stem: A trapezium has parallel sides $6$ cm and $10$ cm, and height $4$ cm. What is its area?

options.why_wrong: Forgets the $\tfrac12$ in the trapezium formula $\tfrac12(a+b)h$.
Uses only the LARGER parallel side ($10\times4$), forgetting to average the two parallel sides first.
Uses only the SMALLER parallel side ($6\times4$), forgetting to average the two parallel sides first.

mcq.explanation: $A=\tfrac12(6+10)\times4=\tfrac12\times16\times4=32\,\text{cm}^2$.

mcq.stem: To find the area of a parallelogram with base $12$ cm and two equal slanted sides of $9$ cm, which further piece of information is needed?

options.text: The length of a slanted side
options.why_wrong: Already given, and not what's needed for area — a slanted side is only used in the PERIMETER, not the area.

options.text: The perpendicular height between the base and the opposite side

options.why_wrong: A diagonal is not part of the area formula $A=bh$. (Knowing a diagonal would let you find the area by a much longer route using trigonometry, but the piece of information the formula needs is the perpendicular height.)
Knowing the perimeter would not reveal the perpendicular height on its own; it is a different piece of information, not a substitute for it.

mcq.explanation: A parallelogram's area formula, $A=bh$, needs the base and the PERPENDICULAR height. The slant side is already given and does not fix the height (the parallelogram can lean more or less), and the perimeter adds nothing new.

mcq.stem: A rectangle has perimeter $36$ cm and its length is three times its width. What is its area?

options.why_wrong: Correctly finds the width ($4.5$) but then squares it, as if the shape were a square rather than a rectangle with a different length.
Drops the factor of $2$ in the perimeter formula, solving $4w=36$ instead of $2(3w+w)=36$, giving a width (and area) far too large.
Finds the width $4.5$ correctly but then takes the length as 'three MORE than' the width ($4.5+3=7.5$) instead of three TIMES it, giving $4.5\times7.5=33.75$.

mcq.explanation: Let the width be $w$: $2(3w+w)=36\Rightarrow8w=36\Rightarrow w=4.5$, length $=13.5$, so $A=4.5\times13.5=60.75\,\text{cm}^2$.

mcq.stem: A triangle has sides $13$ cm, $13$ cm and $10$ cm. The perpendicular height onto the $10$ cm side is $12$ cm. What is the triangle's area?

options.why_wrong: Uses the slanted side $13$ as if it were the height, instead of the given perpendicular height $12$.
Forgets the $\tfrac12$ in the triangle area formula.
Uses the semi-perimeter $(13+13+10)\div2=18$ as if it were the height ($\tfrac12\times10\times18=90$); the height must be the PERPENDICULAR distance, $12$.

mcq.explanation: $A=\tfrac12\times10\times12=60\,\text{cm}^2$, using the given base and its correct perpendicular height.

flashcards.front: Rectangle: $P$, $A$?
flashcards.back: $P=2(l+w)$, $A=lw$. (Square: $P=4a$, $A=a^2$.) Neither is given in the exam.

flashcards.front: Triangle area formula
flashcards.back: $A=\tfrac12bh$, using the PERPENDICULAR height — this one IS given in the exam.

flashcards.front: Parallelogram area formula
flashcards.back: $A=bh$, using the perpendicular height, NOT the slanted side. Not given in the exam.

flashcards.front: Trapezium area formula
flashcards.back: $A=\tfrac12(a+b)h$, where $a,b$ are the parallel sides and $h$ is the perpendicular distance between them. Not given in the exam.

flashcards.front: Which of the rectangle/triangle/parallelogram/trapezium area formulas is in the exam's List of formulas?
flashcards.back: Only the triangle, $A=\tfrac12bh$. The other three must be memorised.

flashcards.front: True or false: a parallelogram's height is the same as its slanted side.
flashcards.back: False. The height is the PERPENDICULAR distance between the base and the opposite side; the slanted side is only used in the perimeter.

flashcards.front: True or false: a triangle's height must always lie inside the triangle.
flashcards.back: False. In an obtuse triangle, the perpendicular height from the opposite vertex can fall OUTSIDE the triangle, on an extension of the base line.

flashcards.front: Triangle vs. parallelogram, same base and height — area relationship?
flashcards.back: The triangle's area is always exactly HALF the parallelogram's: $\tfrac12bh$ versus $bh$.

flashcards.front: Perimeter: what operation, what unit?
flashcards.back: Perimeter is a SUM of all the sides, measured in a LENGTH unit (e.g. cm) — never $\text{cm}^2$.

flashcards.front: Method for a 'working backwards' area or perimeter problem
flashcards.back: Write every side in terms of one letter, form an equation from the given perimeter or area, solve it, then (if needed) substitute back to find what was actually asked for.

flashcards.front: Why is a trapezium's area (average of parallel sides) $\times$ height?
flashcards.back: Two copies of the trapezium, one turned around, fit together into a parallelogram of base (sum of the two parallel sides) and height $h$; one trapezium is exactly half of that parallelogram, giving $\tfrac12(a+b)h$.

flashcards.front: Given a triangle's area and base, how do you find its height?
flashcards.back: Rearrange $A=\tfrac12bh$ to $h=\dfrac{2A}{b}$.

flashcards.front: Sanity range for a trapezium's area
flashcards.back: It must lie strictly between the two rectangles $a\times h$ and $b\times h$ built on its shorter and longer parallel sides.

flashcards.front: Define the 'height' used in any area formula in this lesson.
flashcards.back: The PERPENDICULAR distance from the chosen base to the opposite vertex (triangle) or opposite side (parallelogram/trapezium) — never a slanted side, unless that side happens to meet the base at a right angle.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Computing a triangle's area as $b\times h$, forgetting the $\tfrac12$.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Area is introduced first as 'base times height' for a rectangle, and the extra $\tfrac12$ needed for a triangle is easy to drop under exam pressure, especially once a student has correctly identified the right base and height.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner's triangle-area answer is exactly double a value that is independently known or sense-checked to be correct.
misconceptions.correct_model: A triangle's area is $\tfrac12bh$: it is always exactly HALF the area of a rectangle or parallelogram built on the same base and the same perpendicular height, because two copies of the triangle tile that rectangle or parallelogram exactly.
misconceptions.remediation: Write the formula $A=\tfrac12bh$ out in full before substituting any numbers, and say the $\tfrac12$ out loud as a separate step rather than trying to do it 'in your head' at the end.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Using a SLANTED side of a triangle or parallelogram as if it were the perpendicular height, e.g. using the equal side $13$ instead of the true height $12$ in a triangle with sides $13,13,10$.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: In a right-angled triangle one of the two legs genuinely IS the height, so this habit works until the first non-right-angled shape, where the only lengths given are slanted sides rather than the true perpendicular distance.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner substitutes a side length into the area formula without first checking (or being told) that it is perpendicular to the chosen base.
misconceptions.correct_model: The height used in $A=\tfrac12bh$ (or $A=bh$ for a parallelogram) must be the PERPENDICULAR distance from the base to the opposite vertex or side — a slanted side is only ever usable as the height in the single special case of a right angle between it and the base.
misconceptions.remediation: Before substituting any 'height', check for a right-angle marker between it and the base in the diagram; if none is given, the length is a side, not a height, and a different method (e.g. Pythagoras) may be needed to find the true height first.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Using the slanted side of a parallelogram instead of its perpendicular height, e.g. computing area as base $\times$ slant side ($8.5\times5$) instead of base $\times$ perpendicular height ($8.5\times4$).
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A parallelogram's slant side is often the only other number quoted besides the base, so it feels like the 'other dimension needed' for the area, especially since it IS the right second number needed for the PERIMETER.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner's parallelogram area answer uses the slant side, and matches what would have been needed for a perimeter calculation instead.
misconceptions.correct_model: A parallelogram's area needs base $\times$ PERPENDICULAR height between the base and its opposite side, never the slanted side; the slanted side is only needed for the PERIMETER.
misconceptions.remediation: Before calculating, label clearly which given numbers are needed for area (base, perpendicular height) and which are needed for perimeter (both pairs of sides) — they are rarely the same pair.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Confusing which operation belongs to perimeter and which to area — e.g. adding lengths to find an area, or multiplying lengths to find a perimeter.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Perimeter and area are taught together from the very start, and under time pressure the two different operations (sum of all sides vs. product of base and height) can get swapped, especially in a multi-part question that asks for both.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner's 'area' answer is suspiciously close to a sum of lengths rather than a product, or their 'perimeter' answer looks like a product rather than a sum, and the units quoted don't match (cm vs. $\text{cm}^2$).
misconceptions.correct_model: Perimeter is always a SUM of lengths (units: cm, a length) and area is always built from a PRODUCT of a base and a perpendicular height (units: $\text{cm}^2$, a square measure) — checking the units of your own answer catches this error immediately.
misconceptions.remediation: Before writing a final answer, check its unit against what was asked: a length answer with $\text{cm}^2$ or an area answer with plain cm is an immediate sign the wrong operation was used.

common_mistakes.mistake: Forgetting the $\tfrac12$ in the triangle (or trapezium) area formula.
common_mistakes.why: Area is first learned as 'base times height' for a rectangle, and the extra $\tfrac12$ (or the averaging step in the trapezium) is easy to drop once the right numbers have been correctly identified.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Write the full formula symbolically before substituting any numbers, and treat the $\tfrac12$ (or the averaging) as its own explicit step.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using a slanted side instead of the perpendicular height in a parallelogram or triangle area.
common_mistakes.why: The slanted side is often the only other number given besides the base, so it feels like 'the other dimension needed', even though it is actually needed for the perimeter, not the area.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Before substituting a length as a 'height', check that a right-angle marker connects it to the chosen base in the diagram.

common_mistakes.mistake: Confusing the operations for perimeter (add) and area (multiply), especially in a multi-part question asking for both.
common_mistakes.why: Both quantities are introduced together from the first lesson onward, and under time pressure the two different operations can get swapped.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check the UNIT of every final answer against what was asked: a length answer with $\text{cm}^2$, or an area answer with plain cm, is an immediate sign of the wrong operation.

exam_notes: Only the triangle's area formula, $A=\tfrac12bh$, is printed in the exam's List of formulas; the rectangle, parallelogram and trapezium formulas must be memorised.

Mark (or imagine marking) the perpendicular height with a right-angle symbol in any diagram before substituting it into a formula — this both avoids the slant-side error and shows the examiner your method clearly.

For a 'show that' height or area question, write the substitution explicitly and finish with a concluding sentence stating the required value — stopping at an unsimplified expression loses the final accuracy mark even if the arithmetic is correct.

Always state the correct unit with every answer: cm for a perimeter or a length such as a height, $\text{cm}^2$ for an area — a numerically correct answer with the wrong unit can still lose the final mark.

summary.big_idea: Every area formula in this lesson comes from the rectangle: a parallelogram rearranges into one, a triangle is always exactly half of one, and a trapezium is half of a parallelogram made from two copies of itself — and in every case the 'height' must be the PERPENDICULAR distance to the base, never a slanted side.
key_points: Rectangle: $P=2(l+w)$, $A=lw$. Square: $P=4a$, $A=a^2$. Neither is given in the exam.
Triangle: $A=\tfrac12bh$ (given in the exam); the height is perpendicular to the base and can fall outside an obtuse triangle.
Parallelogram: $A=bh$; trapezium: $A=\tfrac12(a+b)h$ — both use the perpendicular height, never a slanted side, and neither formula is given in the exam.
A slanted side is needed for the PERIMETER of a parallelogram or trapezium, but never for its AREA.
For a missing length, write 'formula $=$ known value' and solve the resulting equation; then substitute back if a further quantity (such as area) was actually asked for.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Every area formula here needs the PERPENDICULAR height, never a slanted side — and a triangle is always exactly half of the parallelogram or rectangle with the same base and height.

epistemic_overrides.note: Every formula comes from the rectangle
A method for every shape in this lesson

03_Circles_Arcs_and_Sectors.json.course_label: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 · Mensuration · Core + Extended
