exercises.statement: Copy and complete the sentences below: (a) There are ... centimetres in one metre. (b) There are ... millimetres in one metre. (c) One metre is one ... of a kilometre. (d) One milligram is one ... of a gram. (e) One thousandth of a litre is one ... .
exercises.answer: (a) 100 cm (b) 1000 mm (c) one thousandth (1/1000) of a kilometre (d) one thousandth (1/1000) of a gram (e) one millilitre
exercises.full_solution: Using the metric definitions given in the text: 1 m = 100 cm, so there are 100 centimetres in a metre. 1 m = 1000 mm, so there are 1000 millimetres in a metre. 1 km = 1000 m, so 1 m = 1/1000 km. 1 g = 1000 mg, so 1 mg = 1/1000 g. 1 litre = 1000 ml, so 1/1000 of a litre = 1 ml.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Which of the units mm, cm, m, km, mg, g, kg, t, ml, litres would be used to measure the following? (a) your height (b) the length of your finger (c) the mass of a shoe (d) the amount of liquid in a cup (e) the height of a van (f) the mass of a ship (g) the capacity of a swimming pool (h) the length of a highway (i) the mass of an elephant (j) the capacity of the petrol tank of a car
exercises.answer: (a) m (b) cm (c) g (d) ml (e) m (f) t (g) litres (h) km (i) kg (j) litres
exercises.full_solution: Each quantity is matched to the most sensible unit of the given type (length, mass or capacity) based on typical real-world size: human height ~1-2 m; a finger ~5-10 cm; a shoe ~200-500 g; a cup of liquid ~200 ml; a van height ~2-3 m; a ship's mass is measured in tonnes; a swimming pool's capacity in litres (though very large, litres is still the standard unit used, sometimes quoted in thousands of litres); a highway's length in km; an elephant's mass in kg (several thousand kg, i.e. a few tonnes, but kg is the base unit normally used before converting to tonnes); a car's petrol tank in litres.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: (a) Change 5.8 km into m. (b) Change 4700 mm to m. (c) Convert 2.3 km into cm.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Put in the missing unit to make the following statements correct: (a) 300 ... = 30 cm (b) 6000 mm = 6 ... (c) 3.2 m = 3200 ... (d) 4.2 ... = 4200 mm (e) 2.5 km = 2500 ...
exercises.full_solution: (a) 300 mm = 30 cm since 10 mm = 1 cm. (b) 6000 mm = 6 m since 1000 mm = 1 m. (c) 3.2 m = 3200 mm since 1 m = 1000 mm. (d) 4.2 m = 4200 mm since 1 m = 1000 mm. (e) 2.5 km = 2500 m since 1 km = 1000 m.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Convert the following to millimetres: (a) 8.5 cm (b) 23 cm (c) 0.83 m (d) 0.05 m (e) 0.004 m
exercises.full_solution: Each length is multiplied by 10 (if in cm) or by 1000 (if in m) to convert to mm: (a) 8.5 × 10 = 85 mm. (b) 23 × 10 = 230 mm. (c) 0.83 × 1000 = 830 mm. (d) 0.05 × 1000 = 50 mm. (e) 0.004 × 1000 = 4 mm.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Convert the following to metres: (a) 560 cm (b) 6.4 km (c) 96 cm (d) 0.004 km (e) 12 mm
exercises.full_solution: Divide by 100 (if in cm) or multiply by 1000 (if in km) or divide by 1000 (if in mm) to convert to m: (a) 560/100 = 5.6 m. (b) 6.4 × 1000 = 6400 m. (c) 96/100 = 0.96 m. (d) 0.004 × 1000 = 4 m. (e) 12/1000 = 0.012 m.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Convert the following to kilometres: (a) 1150 m (b) 250000 m (c) 500 m (d) 70 m (e) 8 m
exercises.full_solution: Divide each length in metres by 1000 to convert to kilometres: (a) 1150/1000 = 1.15 km. (b) 250000/1000 = 250 km. (c) 500/1000 = 0.5 km. (d) 70/1000 = 0.07 km. (e) 8/1000 = 0.008 km.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: (a) Convert 8300 kg to tonnes. (b) Convert 2.5 g to mg.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Since 1000 kg = 1 tonne, 8300 kg = 8300/1000 tonnes = 8.3 tonnes. (b) Since 1 g = 1000 mg, 2.5 g = 2.5 × 1000 mg = 2500 mg.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Convert the following: (a) 3.8 g to mg (b) 28500 kg to tonnes (c) 4.28 tonnes to kg (d) 320 mg to g (e) 0.5 tonnes to kg
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Calculate the following and give the totals in ml: (a) 3 litres + 1500 ml (b) 0.88 litre + 650 ml (c) 0.75 litre + 6300 ml (d) 450 ml + 0.55 litre
exercises.full_solution: Convert each litre amount to ml (1 litre = 1000 ml) then add: (a) 3000 + 1500 = 4500 ml. (b) 880 + 650 = 1530 ml. (c) 750 + 6300 = 7050 ml. (d) 450 + 550 = 1000 ml.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Calculate the following and give the total in litres: (a) 0.75 litre + 450 ml (b) 850 ml + 490 ml (c) 0.6 litre + 0.8 litre (d) 80 ml + 620 ml + 0.7 litre
exercises.full_solution: Convert all amounts to litres (1000 ml = 1 litre) then add: (a) 0.75 + 0.45 = 1.2 litres. (b) 0.85 + 0.49 = 1.34 litres. (c) 0.6 + 0.8 = 1.4 litres. (d) 0.08 + 0.62 + 0.7 = 1.4 litres.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Convert the following areas: (a) 10 m² to cm² (b) 2 m² to mm² (c) 5 km² to m² (d) 3.2 km² to m² (e) 8.3 cm² to mm²
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Convert the following areas: (a) 500 cm² to m² (b) 15000 mm² to cm² (c) 1000 m² to km² (d) 40000 mm² to m² (e) 2500000 cm² to km²
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Convert the following volumes: (a) 2.5 m³ to cm³ (b) 3.4 cm³ to mm³ (c) 2 km³ to m³ (d) 0.2 m³ to cm³ (e) 0.03 m³ to mm³
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Convert the following volumes: (a) 150000 cm³ to m³ (b) 24000 mm³ to cm³ (c) 850000 m³ to km³ (d) 300 mm³ to cm³ (e) 15 cm³ to m³
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Calculate the breadth of a rectangle of area $200\text{ cm}^2$ and length $25$ cm.
exercises.full_solution: Using $A = lb$: $200 = 25b$, so $b = 200/25 = 8$. The breadth is 8 cm.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Calculate the areas of the triangles below: (a) a right-angled triangle with the two perpendicular sides (base and height) measuring 4 cm and 3 cm. (b) a right-angled triangle with the two perpendicular sides (base and height) measuring 13 cm and 5 cm.
exercises.full_solution: Area of a triangle $A = \tfrac{1}{2}bh$. (a) $A = \tfrac12 \times 4 \times 3 = 6\text{ cm}^2$. (b) $A = \tfrac12 \times 13 \times 5 = 32.5\text{ cm}^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Calculate the area of a parallelogram with base length 8 cm and perpendicular height 6 cm.
exercises.full_solution: Area of parallelogram = base length x perpendicular height = $8 \times 6 = 48\text{ cm}^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Calculate the shaded area in a shape consisting of a $12\text{ cm} \times 8\text{ cm}$ rectangle with a trapezium-shaped hole cut from it. The trapezium hole has parallel sides of 3 cm and 5 cm and a perpendicular distance (height) between them of 5 cm.
exercises.full_solution: Area of rectangle $= 12 \times 8 = 96\text{ cm}^2$. Area of trapezium $= \tfrac12 \times 5 \times (3+5) = \tfrac12 \times 5 \times 8 = 20\text{ cm}^2$. Shaded area $= 96 - 20 = 76\text{ cm}^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: The 12 cm by 8 cm rectangle with the trapezium-shaped hole (parallel sides 3 cm and 5 cm, 5 cm apart) cut out of it.

exercises.statement: Find the area of a parallelogram with one pair of parallel sides of length 6.5 cm, and a perpendicular height (measured between the two parallel sides of length 6.5 cm) of 9 cm.
exercises.full_solution: Area of parallelogram = base x perpendicular height $= 6.5 \times 9 = 58.5\text{ cm}^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides of length 13 cm and 8 cm, and a perpendicular height between them of 8 cm.
exercises.full_solution: Area of trapezium $= \tfrac12 h (a+b) = \tfrac12 \times 8 \times (13+8) = \tfrac12 \times 8 \times 21 = 84\text{ cm}^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A pentagon-shaped figure can be split by a vertical line into a rectangle and a trapezium. The rectangle has width 5.5 cm and height 11 cm. The adjoining trapezium (to its left) has two parallel vertical sides of length 7.2 cm and 11 cm, separated by a horizontal distance of 6.4 cm. Find the total area of the figure.
exercises.full_solution: Area of rectangle $= 5.5 \times 11 = 60.5\text{ cm}^2$. Area of trapezium $= \tfrac12 \times 6.4 \times (7.2+11) = \tfrac12 \times 6.4 \times 18.2 = 58.24\text{ cm}^2$. Total area $= 60.5 + 58.24 = 118.74\text{ cm}^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: The pentagon split by a vertical line into a 5.5 cm by 11 cm rectangle and a trapezium whose parallel vertical sides are 7.2 cm and 11 cm, 6.4 cm apart.

exercises.statement: A pentagon-shaped figure is made up of a parallelogram (with a pair of parallel horizontal sides of length 15 cm, separated by a perpendicular height of 7 cm) and an adjoining triangle below it that shares the 15 cm side as its base and also has a perpendicular height of 7 cm. Find the total area of the figure.
exercises.full_solution: Area of parallelogram $= 15 \times 7 = 105\text{ cm}^2$. Area of triangle $= \tfrac12 \times 15 \times 7 = 52.5\text{ cm}^2$. Total area $= 105 + 52.5 = 157.5\text{ cm}^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: The pentagon: a parallelogram of base 15 cm and height 7 cm with a triangle below it on the same 15 cm side, also of height 7 cm.

exercises.statement: A trapezium has area $20\text{ cm}^2$, one parallel side of length 6 cm, and a perpendicular height of 4 cm. Calculate the length $a$ of the other parallel side.
exercises.full_solution: Area $= \tfrac12 h(a+b)$: $20 = \tfrac12 \times 4 \times (a+6) = 2(a+6)$, so $a + 6 = 10$, giving $a = 4$ cm.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A trapezium and a parallelogram are joined along a common edge. The trapezium has parallel sides of 6 cm (top) and 12 cm (bottom, shared with the parallelogram's top side), with a perpendicular height of 4 cm between them. The parallelogram has a base of 12 cm and an unknown perpendicular height $x$ cm. If the areas of the trapezium and the parallelogram are equal, calculate $x$.
exercises.full_solution: Area of trapezium $= \tfrac12 \times 4 \times (6+12) = \tfrac12 \times 4 \times 18 = 36\text{ cm}^2$. Since the parallelogram's top side is shared with the trapezium's bottom side and a parallelogram's opposite sides are equal, the parallelogram's base is also 12 cm. Setting its area equal to the trapezium's area: $12x = 36$, so $x = 3$ cm.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: The trapezium (parallel sides 6 cm and 12 cm, height 4 cm) joined along its 12 cm side to the parallelogram of base 12 cm and height x cm.

exercises.statement: The end view of a house is a quadrilateral (trapezium) with a vertical left side of height 6 m, a vertical right side of height 4 m, and a horizontal base of width 5 m (the top slants from the top of the 6 m side down to the top of the 4 m side). A rectangular door of width 0.75 m and height 2 m is cut out of the brickwork. Calculate the area of brickwork.
exercises.full_solution: The end view is a trapezium with parallel sides 6 m and 4 m, and perpendicular distance (base width) 5 m between them: Area $= \tfrac12 \times 5 \times (6+4) = \tfrac12 \times 5 \times 10 = 25\text{ m}^2$. Area of door $= 0.75 \times 2 = 1.5\text{ m}^2$. Area of brickwork $= 25 - 1.5 = 23.5\text{ m}^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: The end view of the house: a trapezium with vertical sides 6 m and 4 m on a 5 m base, with the doorway removed.

exercises.statement: A garden in the shape of a trapezium (height $8\text{ m}$) is split into three parts: a flower bed in the shape of a right-angled triangle on the left (base $4\text{ m}$, height $8\text{ m}$), a section of grass in the shape of a trapezium in the middle (parallel sides $10\text{ m}$ at the top and $x\text{ m}$ at the bottom, height $8\text{ m}$), and a flower bed in the shape of a parallelogram on the right (base $3\text{ m}$ along the bottom, height $8\text{ m}$). The area of the grass is two and a half times the total area of the flower beds. Calculate: (a) the area of each flower bed, (b) the area of grass, (c) the value of $x$.
exercises.answer: (a) Triangular flower bed $=16\text{ m}^2$, parallelogram flower bed $=24\text{ m}^2$ (total $40\text{ m}^2$) (b) Grass area $=100\text{ m}^2$ (c) $x=15$
exercises.full_solution: Triangle area $=\tfrac12\times4\times8=16\text{ m}^2$. Parallelogram area $=$ base $\times$ height $=3\times8=24\text{ m}^2$. Total flower bed area $=16+24=40\text{ m}^2$. Grass area $=2.5\times40=100\text{ m}^2$. The grass is a trapezium with parallel sides $10\text{ m}$ and $x\text{ m}$ and height $8\text{ m}$: $\tfrac12\times8\times(10+x)=100\Rightarrow4(10+x)=100\Rightarrow10+x=25\Rightarrow x=15$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: The garden: a triangular flower bed (base 4 m), the trapezium of grass (parallel sides 10 m and x m) and a parallelogram-shaped flower bed (base 3 m), all of height 8 m.

exercises.statement: (a) Calculate the circumference of a circle of radius 3 cm, giving your answer to 3 s.f. and also in exact form. (b) If the circumference of a circle is 12 cm, calculate the radius, giving your answer (i) to 3 s.f. (ii) in terms of $\pi$. (c) Calculate the area of a circle of radius 5 cm, giving your answer (i) to 3 s.f. (ii) in exact form. (d) The area of a circle is $34\text{ cm}^2$; calculate the radius, giving your answer (i) to 3 s.f. (ii) in terms of $\pi$.
exercises.full_solution: (a) $C = 2\pi r = 2\pi \times 3 = 6\pi = 18.8$ cm (3 s.f.). (b) $r = C/(2\pi) = 12/(2\pi) = 1.91$ cm (3 s.f.), or exactly $r = 6/\pi$ cm. (c) $A = \pi r^2 = \pi \times 5^2 = 25\pi = 78.5\text{ cm}^2$ (3 s.f.), exact $25\pi\text{ cm}^2$. (d) $r = \sqrt{A/\pi} = \sqrt{34/\pi} = 3.29$ cm (3 s.f.), exact $\sqrt{34/\pi}$ cm. All values verified with $\pi = 3.14159...$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
exercises.source_label: Worked examples (circumference & area of a circle), a-d

exercises.statement: Four circles are shown: (a) radius $4\text{ cm}$ (b) radius $3.5\text{ cm}$ (c) diameter $9.2\text{ cm}$ (d) diameter $0.5\text{ m}$. Calculate: Q1 the circumference of each circle, to 3 s.f.; Q2 the area of each circle, to 3 s.f.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Calculate the radius of a circle when the circumference is: (a) 15 cm (b) $\pi$ cm (c) 4 m (d) 8 mm
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Calculate the diameter of a circle when the area is: (a) $16\text{ cm}^2$ (b) $9\pi\text{ cm}^2$ (c) $8.2\text{ m}^2$ (d) $14.6\text{ mm}^2$
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: The wheel of a car has an outer radius of 25 cm. Calculate: (a) how far the car has travelled after one complete turn of the wheel, (b) how many times the wheel turns for a journey of 1 km.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Distance per turn = circumference $= 2\pi \times 25 = 157.1$ cm (3 s.f.). (b) $1\text{ km} = 100000$ cm. Number of turns $= 100000 / 157.08 = 636.6$, i.e. about 637 turns.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: If the wheel of a bicycle has a diameter of 60 cm, calculate how far a cyclist will have travelled after the wheel has rotated 100 times.
exercises.full_solution: Circumference $= \pi d = \pi \times 60 = 188.5$ cm. Distance for 100 rotations $= 100 \times 188.5 = 18850$ cm $\approx 18800$ cm (3 s.f.), i.e. 188 m.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A circular ring has outer radius 22 mm and inner radius 20 mm. Calculate the cross-sectional area of the ring, giving your answer in terms of $\pi$.
exercises.full_solution: Area of ring = area of outer circle $-$ area of inner circle $= \pi(22^2 - 20^2) = \pi(484 - 400) = 84\pi\text{ mm}^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Four circles of radius 3 cm are drawn in a line and enclosed by a rectangle. Calculate the unshaded area within the rectangle, giving your answer in exact form.
exercises.full_solution: The rectangle has width $4 \times (2\times3) = 24$ cm and height $2\times3 = 6$ cm, so rectangle area $= 24\times6 = 144\text{ cm}^2$. Total area of the 4 circles $= 4 \times \pi \times 3^2 = 36\pi\text{ cm}^2$. Unshaded area $= 144 - 36\pi\text{ cm}^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: Four touching circles of radius 3 cm in a line inside the smallest rectangle that encloses them, 24 cm by 6 cm. The unshaded area is the rectangle minus the four circles.

exercises.statement: (a) Calculate the surface area of a cuboid measuring $7\text{ cm} \times 10\text{ cm} \times 5\text{ cm}$. (b) Calculate the surface area of a cylinder of radius 3 cm and height 7 cm, giving your answer to 3 s.f.
exercises.full_solution: (a) $SA = 2(lw+lh+wh) = 2(7\times10 + 7\times5 + 10\times5) = 2(70+35+50) = 2 \times 155 = 310\text{ cm}^2$. (b) $SA = 2\pi r(r+h) = 2\pi \times 3 \times (3+7) = 2\pi\times3\times10 = 60\pi = 188.5\text{ cm}^2 \approx 188\text{ cm}^2$ (3 s.f.).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
exercises.source_label: Worked examples (surface area of cuboid & cylinder)

exercises.statement:
Q1: Calculate the surface area of each cuboid: (a) $l=12$ cm, $w=10$ cm, $h=5$ cm (b) $l=4$ cm, $w=6$ cm, $h=8$ cm (c) $l=4.2$ cm, $w=7.1$ cm, $h=3.9$ cm (d) $l=5.2$ cm, $w=2.1$ cm, $h=0.8$ cm.
Q2: Calculate the height of each cuboid: (a) $l=5$ cm, $w=6$ cm, surface area $104\text{ cm}^2$ (b) $l=2$ cm, $w=8$ cm, surface area $112\text{ cm}^2$ (c) $l=3.5$ cm, $w=4$ cm, surface area $118\text{ cm}^2$ (d) $l=4.2$ cm, $w=10$ cm, surface area $226\text{ cm}^2$.
Q3: Calculate the surface area of each cylinder: (a) $r=2$ cm, $h=6$ cm (b) $r=4$ cm, $h=7$ cm (c) $r=3.5$ cm, $h=9.2$ cm (d) $r=0.8$ cm, $h=4.3$ cm.
Q4: Calculate the height of each cylinder, to 1 d.p.: (a) $r=2.0$ cm, surface area $40\text{ cm}^2$ (b) $r=3.5$ cm, surface area $88\text{ cm}^2$ (c) $r=5.5$ cm, surface area $250\text{ cm}^2$ (d) $r=3.0$ cm, surface area $189\text{ cm}^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Q1: The edges of the larger of two cubes are 4 cm long. The ratio of their surface areas is 1:4. Calculate (a) the surface area of the small cube, (b) the length of an edge of the small cube. Q2: A cube of edge 6 cm has the same surface area as a cylinder of radius 2 cm; find the cylinder's height. Q3: Two cylinders have the same surface area; one has radius 3 cm and height 2 cm, the other has radius 1 cm; find its height. Q4: Two cuboids have the same surface area; one measures $3\text{ cm}\times4\text{ cm}\times2\text{ cm}$, the other has length 1 cm and width 4 cm; find its height.
exercises.full_solution: Q1: (a) Surface area of the large cube $=6\times4^2=96\text{ cm}^2$, so the small cube has $96\div4=24\text{ cm}^2$. (b) Each face of the small cube has area $24\div6=4\text{ cm}^2$, so its edge is $\sqrt4=2$ cm. Q2: $SA_{cube}=6\times6^2=216\text{ cm}^2$. For cylinder: $2\pi\times2\times(2+h)=216 \Rightarrow 2+h = 216/(4\pi) = 17.19 \Rightarrow h \approx 15.2$ cm (verified using $SA=2\pi r(r+h)$). Q3: $SA_1 = 2\pi\times3\times(3+2)=30\pi\text{ cm}^2$. For the second cylinder: $2\pi\times1\times(1+h)=30\pi \Rightarrow 1+h=15 \Rightarrow h=14$ cm. Q4: $SA=2(3\times4+3\times2+4\times2)=2(12+6+8)=52\text{ cm}^2$. For the second cuboid: $2(1\times4+1\times h+4h)=52 \Rightarrow 2(4+5h)=52 \Rightarrow 4+5h=26 \Rightarrow h=4.4$ cm. (Each part uses straightforward rearrangement of the surface-area formula for the given solid.)
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: (a) Calculate the volume of a cylinder of radius 4 cm and length 10 cm, giving your answer in terms of $\pi$. (b) An L-shaped prism has a cross-section made of two rectangles: rectangle A is $5\text{ cm}\times2\text{ cm}$ and rectangle B is $5\text{ cm}\times1\text{ cm}$. The prism has length 5 cm. Calculate (i) the volume and (ii) the total surface area of the prism.
exercises.full_solution: (a) $V = \pi r^2 l = \pi\times4^2\times10 = 160\pi\text{ cm}^3 \approx 503\text{ cm}^3$ (3 s.f.). (b) Cross-sectional area $= A_A + A_B = (5\times2) + (5\times1) = 10+5 = 15\text{ cm}^2$. Volume $= 15\times5 = 75\text{ cm}^3$. For the surface area, the two L-shaped ends each contribute $15\text{ cm}^2$ ($2\times15=30\text{ cm}^2$), and the six edges of the L-shape (with the prism's length of 5 cm as the extra dimension) contribute the remaining rectangular faces, whose combined area is $110\text{ cm}^2$; total surface area $= 30+110 = 140\text{ cm}^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
exercises.source_label: Worked examples (volume & surface area of prisms)

exercises.statement:
Q1: Calculate the volume of each cuboid, where $w$, $l$ and $h$ are the width, length and height: (a) $w=2$ cm, $l=3$ cm, $h=4$ cm (b) $w=6$ cm, $l=1$ cm, $h=3$ cm (c) $w=6$ cm, $l=23$ mm, $h=2$ cm (d) $w=42$ mm, $l=3$ cm, $h=0.007$ m.
Q2: Calculate the volume of each cylinder, where $r$ is the radius of the circular face and $h$ the height: (a) $r=4$ cm, $h=9$ cm (b) $r=3.5$ cm, $h=7.2$ cm (c) $r=25$ mm, $h=10$ cm (d) $r=0.3$ cm, $h=17$ mm.
exercises.answer: Q1: (a) $24\text{ cm}^3$ (b) $18\text{ cm}^3$ (c) $27.6\text{ cm}^3$ (d) $8.82\text{ cm}^3$. Q2: (a) $144\pi\approx452\text{ cm}^3$ (b) $88.2\pi\approx277\text{ cm}^3$ (c) $62.5\pi\approx196\text{ cm}^3$ (d) $0.153\pi\approx0.481\text{ cm}^3$.
exercises.full_solution:
Convert to the same unit (cm) first. Q1: $V=lwh$. (a) $2\times3\times4=24\text{ cm}^3$. (b) $6\times1\times3=18\text{ cm}^3$. (c) $l=23\text{ mm}=2.3$ cm: $6\times2.3\times2=27.6\text{ cm}^3$. (d) $w=42\text{ mm}=4.2$ cm, $h=0.007\text{ m}=0.7$ cm: $4.2\times3\times0.7=8.82\text{ cm}^3$.
Q2: $V=\pi r^2h$. (a) $\pi\times4^2\times9=144\pi\approx452\text{ cm}^3$. (b) $\pi\times3.5^2\times7.2=88.2\pi\approx277\text{ cm}^3$. (c) $r=25\text{ mm}=2.5$ cm: $\pi\times2.5^2\times10=62.5\pi\approx196\text{ cm}^3$. (d) $h=17\text{ mm}=1.7$ cm: $\pi\times0.3^2\times1.7=0.153\pi\approx0.481\text{ cm}^3$ (3 s.f.).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A prism has length 8 cm, and its cross-section is a right-angled triangle with legs 3 cm and 4 cm (and hypotenuse 5 cm). (a) Calculate the volume and total surface area of this prism. A second prism has length 8.2 cm, and its cross-section is an isosceles triangle with a right angle between its two equal sides of 5.0 cm each (so its third side, opposite the right angle, is $\sqrt{5^2+5^2}=7.1$ cm to 1 d.p.). (b) Calculate the volume and total surface area of this second prism.
exercises.answer: (a) Volume $=48\text{ cm}^3$, surface area $=108\text{ cm}^2$. (b) Volume $=102.5\text{ cm}^3$, surface area $=165.22\text{ cm}^2$ (2 d.p.)
exercises.full_solution: (a) Cross-sectional area $=\tfrac12\times3\times4=6\text{ cm}^2$. Volume $=6\times8=48\text{ cm}^3$. Perimeter of triangle $=3+4+5=12$ cm. Surface area $= 2(6) + 12\times8 = 12+96=108\text{ cm}^2$. (b) Cross-sectional area $=\tfrac12\times5\times5=12.5\text{ cm}^2$. Volume $=12.5\times8.2=102.5\text{ cm}^3$. Perimeter of triangle $=5+5+7.1=17.1$ cm. Surface area $=2(12.5)+17.1\times8.2=25+140.22=165.22\text{ cm}^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Calculate the volume of each of the following composite prisms, each of length (depth) as marked: (a) A cuboid cross-section $4\text{ cm}\times4\text{ cm}$ with a rectangular notch $2\text{ cm}$ wide and $1\text{ cm}$ high removed from the middle of the bottom edge; prism length 5 cm. (b) A staircase-shaped cross-section of 3 equal steps, each with riser (height) 2 cm and tread (width) 1 cm; prism length (depth) 8 cm. (c) A pentagon ('house-shaped') cross-section made of a $5\text{ cm}\times7\text{ cm}$ rectangle topped by a triangle of base 5 cm and height 5 cm (total cross-section height 12 cm); prism length (depth) 8 cm. (d) A trapezium cross-section with parallel sides 7 cm and 4 cm and height 5 cm; prism length (depth) 5 cm.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Cross-sectional area $= (4\times4) - (2\times1) = 16-2=14\text{ cm}^2$. Volume $=14\times5=70\text{ cm}^3$. (b) The staircase cross-section is made of three columns of width $1$ cm and heights $2$, $4$ and $6$ cm, so its area $=1\times(2+4+6)=12\text{ cm}^2$. Volume $=12\times8=96\text{ cm}^3$. (c) Cross-sectional area $= (5\times7) + (\tfrac12\times5\times5) = 35+12.5=47.5\text{ cm}^2$. Volume $=47.5\times8=380\text{ cm}^3$. (d) Cross-sectional area $=\tfrac12\times5\times(7+4)=27.5\text{ cm}^2$. Volume $=27.5\times5=137.5\text{ cm}^3$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: The four cross-sections (a) to (d), with each prism length written underneath. All lengths are in centimetres.

exercises.statement: The diagram shows a plan view of a cylinder inside a box in the shape of a cube. The cylinder fits exactly: its radius is $8\text{ cm}$ and its height equals the side of the cube. Calculate the percentage of the volume of the cube that is NOT occupied by the cylinder.
exercises.full_solution: The cube has side $2\times8=16$ cm, so its volume is $16^3=4096\text{ cm}^3$. The cylinder has radius $8$ cm and height $16$ cm: volume $=\pi\times8^2\times16=1024\pi\approx3217\text{ cm}^3$. Unoccupied volume $=4096-3217=879\text{ cm}^3$. Percentage $=\dfrac{879}{4096}\times100\approx21.5\%$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A chocolate bar's cross-section is a hexagonal pack made from 6 identical equilateral triangles, each of base 4 cm and perpendicular height 3.5 cm, arranged around a centre point. The pack has length 20 cm. Calculate: (a) the cross-sectional area of the pack, (b) the volume of the pack.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Area of one triangle $= \tfrac12\times4\times3.5=7\text{ cm}^2$. Total cross-sectional area $= 6\times7=42\text{ cm}^2$. (b) Volume $=42\times20=840\text{ cm}^3$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: The hexagonal cross-section of the pack, made of six identical triangles of base 4 cm and height 3.5 cm around the centre.

exercises.statement: A cylinder of radius 2.5 cm and height 8 cm has the same volume as a cuboid of length 5 cm and width 5 cm. Calculate the height of the cuboid, to 1 decimal place.
exercises.full_solution: Volume of cylinder $=\pi r^2 h = \pi\times2.5^2\times8 = 50\pi \approx 157.08\text{ cm}^3$. For the cuboid: $5\times5\times h = 157.08 \Rightarrow 25h=157.08 \Rightarrow h = 6.3$ cm (1 d.p.).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A steel pipe has inner radius 35 cm, outer radius 36 cm, and length 130 m. Calculate the volume of steel used to make the pipe, giving your answer in terms of $\pi$ (in cm$^3$).
exercises.full_solution: Length $=130\text{ m} = 13000\text{ cm}$. Volume of steel $= \pi(R^2-r^2)\times l = \pi(36^2-35^2)\times13000 = \pi(1296-1225)\times13000 = \pi\times71\times13000 = 923000\pi\text{ cm}^3$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: (a) Calculate the length of an arc which subtends an angle of $80°$ at the centre of a circle of radius 6 cm, giving your answer to 3 s.f. and in exact ($\pi$) form. (b) A minor arc of length 12.4 cm lies on a circle of radius 7 cm. Calculate (i) the angle subtended by the minor arc at the centre, to 1 d.p., (ii) the length of the corresponding major arc.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Arc length $= \tfrac{\theta}{360}\times2\pi r = \tfrac{80}{360}\times2\pi\times6 = \tfrac{8}{3}\pi = 8.38$ cm (3 s.f.). (b)(i) $\theta = \dfrac{\text{arc}}{2\pi r}\times360 = \dfrac{12.4}{2\pi\times7}\times360 = 101.5°$ (1 d.p.). (ii) Full circumference $= 2\pi\times7 = 43.98$ cm; major arc $= 43.98 - 12.4 = 31.6$ cm (3 s.f.).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Calculate the length of the arc, to 3 s.f., for a sector with: (a) angle $45°$, radius 8 cm. (b) angle $8°$, radius 15 cm. (c) angle $110°$, radius 6 cm. (d) angle $270°$ (reflex), radius 5 cm.
exercises.full_solution: Arc length $=\tfrac{\theta}{360}\times2\pi r$. (a) $\tfrac{45}{360}\times2\pi\times8=6.28$ cm. (b) $\tfrac{8}{360}\times2\pi\times15=2.09$ cm. (c) $\tfrac{110}{360}\times2\pi\times6=11.5$ cm. (d) $\tfrac{270}{360}\times2\pi\times5=23.6$ cm. All to 3 s.f.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Q2: Calculate the angle at the centre (to the nearest degree, or as specified) for a sector with arc length $a$ and radius $r$: (a) $r=14$, $a=8$. (b) $r=4$, $a=16$. (c) $r=7.5$, $a=7.5$. (d) $r=6.8$, $a=13.6$. Q3: Calculate the radius for a sector with angle $\phi$ and arc length $a$: (a) $\phi=75°$, $a=16$. (b) $\phi=300°$, $a=24$. (c) $\phi=20°$, $a=6.5$. (d) $\phi=243°$, $a=17$.
exercises.full_solution: Q2 uses $\theta = \dfrac{a}{2\pi r}\times360$: (a) $\dfrac{8}{2\pi\times14}\times360=32.7°$. (b) $\dfrac{16}{2\pi\times4}\times360=229°$. (c) $\dfrac{7.5}{2\pi\times7.5}\times360=57.3°$. (d) $\dfrac{13.6}{2\pi\times6.8}\times360=114.6°$. Q3 uses $r=\dfrac{a\times360}{2\pi\theta}$: (a) $\dfrac{16\times360}{2\pi\times75}=12.2$ cm. (b) $\dfrac{24\times360}{2\pi\times300}=4.58$ cm. (c) $\dfrac{6.5\times360}{2\pi\times20}=18.6$ cm. (d) $\dfrac{17\times360}{2\pi\times243}=4.01$ cm.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: (a) A 'bowtie' shape is formed by two straight lines crossing at a point $O$. On one side, a sector of radius 12 cm is marked with angle $50°$ at $O$; on the opposite side (vertically opposite angle, also $50°$), a sector of radius 5 cm is marked. The shape's perimeter consists of the four straight radii (two of 12 cm, two of 5 cm) plus the two arcs. Calculate the exact perimeter of the shape, in terms of $\pi$. (b) A shape is made of two quarter circles with the same centre $O$ on a straight baseline: a large one of radius $R$ on the left and a small one of radius $r$ on the right. They are joined by a vertical straight edge of length $12$ cm (so $R-r=12$), and the total baseline is $36$ cm (so $R+r=36$). Find $R$ and $r$, and hence calculate the exact perimeter of the shape.
exercises.answer: (a) Perimeter $=\left(34+\dfrac{85\pi}{18}\right)$ cm $\approx 48.8$ cm. (b) $R=24$ cm, $r=12$ cm; Perimeter $=(48+18\pi)$ cm $\approx 104.5$ cm.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Each pair of radii contributes $2\times12+2\times5=34$ cm. Arc for the 12 cm sector: $\tfrac{50}{360}\times2\pi\times12=\tfrac{10\pi}{3}$ cm. Arc for the 5 cm sector: $\tfrac{50}{360}\times2\pi\times5=\tfrac{25\pi}{18}$ cm. Total perimeter $=34+\tfrac{10\pi}{3}+\tfrac{25\pi}{18}=34+\tfrac{60\pi+25\pi}{18}=34+\tfrac{85\pi}{18}$ cm $\approx 48.8$ cm. (b) From $R-r=12$ and $R+r=36$: adding gives $2R=48$, so $R=24$ cm and $r=12$ cm. Perimeter $=$ baseline $(36)$ + vertical edge $(12)$ + large quarter arc $\left(\tfrac{90}{360}\times2\pi\times24=12\pi\right)$ + small quarter arc $\left(\tfrac{90}{360}\times2\pi\times12=6\pi\right)=48+18\pi$ cm $\approx104.5$ cm.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: Part (a): the bowtie made of two vertically opposite sectors of angle 50 degrees and radii 12 cm and 5 cm. Part (b): the two quarter circles on one baseline, joined by the 12 cm vertical edge.

exercises.statement: An annular sector (a sector-shaped 'ring slice') has an outer radius of 24 cm. The OUTER arc has length 20 cm and the INNER arc has length 10 cm (both arcs subtend the same angle $\phi$ at the common centre). Calculate: (a) the inner radius, (b) the perimeter of the shape, (c) the angle $\phi$, to 1 d.p.
exercises.full_solution: Since both arcs subtend the same angle, arc length is proportional to radius: $\dfrac{\text{inner arc}}{\text{inner radius}}=\dfrac{\text{outer arc}}{\text{outer radius}}$, so inner radius $= \dfrac{10\times24}{20}=12$ cm. (b) Perimeter $=$ outer arc $+$ inner arc $+ 2\times(\text{outer radius}-\text{inner radius}) = 20+10+2\times(24-12)=20+10+24=54$ cm. (c) $\phi = \dfrac{\text{outer arc}}{2\pi\times\text{outer radius}}\times360 = \dfrac{20\times360}{2\pi\times24} \approx 47.7°$. (Figure interpretation: the two numbers 20 cm and 10 cm are taken as arc lengths rather than radii, consistent with the convention used in the worked the earlier exercise in this bank of this same section, where arc lengths are explicitly labelled near the curves.)
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: The ring slice: the two arcs subtend the same angle at O, and the two straight edges are each the difference of the radii.

exercises.statement: (a) Calculate the area of a sector of angle $45°$ and radius 12 cm, giving your answer to 3 s.f. and in exact ($\pi$) form. (b) A sector has area $50\text{ cm}^2$ and angle $30°$; calculate its radius, to 3 s.f.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Sector area $=\tfrac{\theta}{360}\times\pi r^2 = \tfrac{45}{360}\times\pi\times12^2 = \tfrac18\times144\pi = 18\pi = 56.5\text{ cm}^2$ (3 s.f.). (b) $50 = \tfrac{30}{360}\times\pi r^2 \Rightarrow r^2 = \dfrac{50\times12}{\pi} = \dfrac{600}{\pi} \Rightarrow r = \sqrt{600/\pi} = 13.8$ cm (3 s.f.).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Q1: Calculate the area of a sector (to 3 s.f.) given angle $\phi$ and radius $r$: (a) $\phi=60°,r=8$ (b) $\phi=120°,r=14$ (c) $\phi=2°,r=18$ (d) $\phi=320°,r=4$. Q2: Calculate the radius (to 3 s.f.) given angle $\phi$ and area $A$: (a) $\phi=40°,A=120\text{ cm}^2$ (b) $\phi=12°,A=42\text{ cm}^2$ (c) $\phi=150°,A=4\text{ cm}^2$ (d) $\phi=300°,A=400\text{ cm}^2$. Q3: Calculate the angle $\phi$ (to the nearest degree) given radius $r$ and area $A$: (a) $r=12\text{ cm},A=60\text{ cm}^2$ (b) $r=26\text{ cm},A=0.02\text{ m}^2$ (c) $r=0.32\text{ m},A=180\text{ cm}^2$ (d) $r=38\text{ mm},A=16\text{ cm}^2$.
exercises.full_solution: Q1 uses $A=\tfrac{\phi}{360}\pi r^2$ directly. Q2 rearranges to $r=\sqrt{\dfrac{360A}{\phi\pi}}$. Q3 rearranges to $\phi=\dfrac{360A}{\pi r^2}$, after converting all lengths/areas to consistent units (e.g. (b) $A=0.02\text{ m}^2=200\text{ cm}^2$, $r=26$ cm; (c) $r=0.32\text{ m}=32$ cm, $A=180\text{ cm}^2$; (d) $r=38\text{ mm}=3.8$ cm, $A=16\text{ cm}^2$, giving $\phi=\dfrac{360\times16}{\pi\times3.8^2}\approx 127°$).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A rotating sprinkler is placed in one corner of a rectangular garden measuring $12\text{ m}$ by $8\text{ m}$. It has a reach of $8\text{ m}$ and rotates through an angle of $30^\circ$, so it waters a sector of radius $8\text{ m}$ and angle $30^\circ$ centred at that corner. Calculate the area of the garden NOT being watered, giving your answer in terms of $\pi$.
exercises.full_solution: Area of garden $=12\times8=96\text{ m}^2$. Area watered (sector) $=\tfrac{30}{360}\times\pi\times8^2=\tfrac{1}{12}\times64\pi=\tfrac{16}{3}\pi\text{ m}^2$. Area not watered $=96-\tfrac{16}{3}\pi\text{ m}^2 \approx 79.2\text{ m}^2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: The 12 m by 8 m garden with the watered sector of radius 8 m and angle 30 degrees at one corner.

exercises.statement: Two sectors $AOB$ and $COD$ share the same centre $O$ and the same angle of $60°$. $OA=15$ cm. The area of sector $AOB$ is three times the area of sector $COD$. Calculate: (a) the area of sector $AOB$, in terms of $\pi$; (b) the area of sector $COD$, in terms of $\pi$; (c) the radius $OC$, to 3 s.f.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Area of $AOB=\tfrac{60}{360}\times\pi\times15^2=\tfrac16\times225\pi=37.5\pi\text{ cm}^2$. (b) Area of $COD=\dfrac{37.5\pi}{3}=12.5\pi\text{ cm}^2$. (c) $12.5\pi=\tfrac{60}{360}\times\pi\times r^2=\tfrac16\pi r^2 \Rightarrow r^2=75 \Rightarrow r=\sqrt{75}=5\sqrt3\approx8.66$ cm.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: The two sectors AOB and COD: the same centre O and the same angle of 60 degrees, with OC shorter than OA.

exercises.statement: (a) Calculate the volume of a sphere of radius 3 cm, to 3 s.f., and in exact ($\pi$) form. (b) A sphere has volume $150\text{ cm}^3$; calculate its radius, to 3 s.f.
exercises.full_solution: (a) $V=\tfrac43\pi r^3 = \tfrac43\pi\times27=36\pi=113\text{ cm}^3$ (3 s.f.). (b) $150=\tfrac43\pi r^3 \Rightarrow r^3=\dfrac{150\times3}{4\pi}=\dfrac{450}{4\pi} \Rightarrow r=\sqrt[3]{450/(4\pi)}=3.30$ cm (3 s.f.).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Q1: Calculate the volume of a sphere (to 3 s.f.) of radius (a) 6 cm (b) 9.5 cm (c) 8.2 cm (d) 0.7 m. Q2: Calculate the radius of a sphere, giving your answers in centimetres and to 1 d.p., with volume (a) $130\text{ cm}^3$ (b) $720\text{ cm}^3$ (c) $0.2\text{ m}^3$ (d) $1000\text{ mm}^3$.
exercises.full_solution: Q1 uses $V=\tfrac43\pi r^3$ directly for each radius. Q2 rearranges to $r=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{3V}{4\pi}}$, with every volume first written in $\text{cm}^3$: (c) $0.2\text{ m}^3=200\,000\text{ cm}^3$, so $r=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{600\,000}{4\pi}}\approx36.3$ cm; (d) $1000\text{ mm}^3=1\text{ cm}^3$, so $r=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{3}{4\pi}}\approx0.6$ cm.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Q1: Sphere $B$ has twice the volume of sphere $A$, which has radius 5 cm. Find the radius of sphere $B$. Q2: A hemispherical bowl has inner radius 5 cm and outer radius 5.5 cm; find the volume of material used, in terms of $\pi$. Q3: A sphere of radius 7 cm is melted down and recast as a hemispherical bowl of inner radius 10 cm; find the outer radius of the bowl. Q4: A ball of radius 10 cm fits exactly inside a cubical box of side 20 cm; find the percentage of the box's volume that is empty. Q5: A steel ball of radius 20 cm is melted down and recast into 8 identical smaller balls; find the radius of each smaller ball, in mm. Q6: A sphere of volume $600\text{ cm}^3$ is cut into 3 pieces and remoulded into 3 new balls $A$, $B$, $C$ with volumes in the ratio $7:5:3$. Find the radius of each new ball. Q7: A cylinder and a sphere have the same radius $r$, and the cylinder's height equals the sphere's diameter ($2r$). Find the ratio of the cylinder's volume to the sphere's volume, in its simplest form.
exercises.answer: Q1: $r_B \approx 6.30$ cm. Q2: material volume $=\tfrac23\pi(5.5^3-5^3)=\dfrac{331}{12}\pi\text{ cm}^3$ ($\approx27.6\pi\approx86.7\text{ cm}^3$). Q3: outer radius $\approx 11.9$ cm. Q4: $\approx 47.6\%$ empty. Q5: $10$ cm $=100$ mm. Q6: $r_A\approx4.1$ cm, $r_B\approx3.6$ cm, $r_C\approx3.1$ cm (to 1 d.p.). Q7: ratio $3:2$.
exercises.full_solution: Q1: $V_B=2V_A \Rightarrow r_B = r_A\times2^{1/3}=5\times1.2599=6.30$ cm. Q2: material volume $=\tfrac23\pi(5.5^3-5^3)=\tfrac23\pi(166.375-125)=\tfrac23\pi\times41.375=\dfrac{331}{12}\pi\text{ cm}^3$. Q3: $\tfrac43\pi\times7^3=\tfrac23\pi(r^3-10^3) \Rightarrow 2\times343=r^3-1000 \Rightarrow r^3=1686 \Rightarrow r=\sqrt[3]{1686}\approx11.9$ cm. Q4: box volume $=20^3=8000\text{ cm}^3$; ball volume $=\tfrac43\pi\times10^3\approx4188.8\text{ cm}^3$; empty $=8000-4188.8=3811.2$, percentage $=3811.2/8000\times100\approx47.6\%$. Q5: since volume scales as $r^3$ and 8 equal balls are formed, each has volume $V/8$, so $r_{small}=R/8^{1/3}=R/2=20/2=10$ cm $=100$ mm. Q6: total volume 600 split into 15 parts: $A=600\times7/15=280$, $B=600\times5/15=200$, $C=600\times3/15=120\text{ cm}^3$; then $r=\sqrt[3]{3V/(4\pi)}$ for each, giving $r_A\approx4.1$ cm, $r_B\approx3.6$ cm, $r_C\approx3.1$ cm (1 d.p.). Q7: $V_{cyl}=\pi r^2(2r)=2\pi r^3$; $V_{sph}=\tfrac43\pi r^3$; ratio $=2:\tfrac43=6:4=3:2$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Q1: Calculate the surface area of a sphere (to 3 s.f.) of radius (a) 6 cm (b) 4.5 cm (c) 12.25 cm (d) $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt\pi}$ cm. Q2: Calculate the radius of a sphere (to 3 s.f.) given surface area (a) $50\text{ cm}^2$ (b) $16.5\text{ cm}^2$ (c) $120\text{ mm}^2$ (d) $\pi\text{ cm}^2$. Q3: Two spheres have radii 8 cm and 16 cm. Express the ratio of their surface areas in the form $1:n$.
exercises.full_solution: Q1 and Q2 use $SA=4\pi r^2$ and its rearrangement $r=\sqrt{SA/(4\pi)}$ directly (note: for Q1(d), $r=1/\sqrt\pi \Rightarrow SA=4\pi\times(1/\pi)=4\text{ cm}^2$ exactly). Q3: ratio of surface areas $=8^2:16^2=64:256=1:4$ (surface area scales with the square of the radius ratio, $16/8=2 \Rightarrow n=2^2=4$).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A solid is formed by placing a hemisphere (radius 5 cm) on one end of a cylinder of the same radius 5 cm, so that the hemisphere caps that end smoothly; the other end of the cylinder is left as a flat circular face. The total length of the solid (cylinder plus hemisphere) is 20 cm. Calculate the total surface area of the solid, in terms of $\pi$.
exercises.full_solution: Cylinder length $= 20 - 5 = 15$ cm (since the hemisphere's radius of 5 cm accounts for the remaining length). Curved surface area of cylinder $=2\pi r l = 2\pi\times5\times15=150\pi$. Curved surface area of hemisphere $=2\pi r^2=2\pi\times25=50\pi$. Flat circular face at the open end $=\pi r^2=25\pi$. Total $=150\pi+50\pi+25\pi=225\pi\text{ cm}^2 \approx 707\text{ cm}^2$ (3 s.f.).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A sphere and a cylinder have the same surface area. The cylinder's height is 16 cm, and this also equals the sphere's diameter (so the sphere's radius is 8 cm). Calculate the radius of the cylinder, to 3 s.f.
exercises.full_solution: Surface area of sphere $=4\pi\times8^2=256\pi\text{ cm}^2$. Setting the cylinder's surface area equal: $2\pi r(r+16)=256\pi \Rightarrow r^2+16r-128=0$. Solving this quadratic: $r=\dfrac{-16+\sqrt{16^2+4\times128}}{2}=\dfrac{-16+\sqrt{768}}{2}\approx5.86$ cm (taking the positive root).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: (a) Calculate the volume of a pyramid with a rectangular base $3\text{ cm}\times7\text{ cm}$ and height 5 cm. (b) A pyramid has a triangular base of area $20\text{ cm}^2$ and volume $60\text{ cm}^3$; calculate its height.
exercises.full_solution: (a) $V=\tfrac13\times\text{base area}\times h = \tfrac13\times(3\times7)\times5=\tfrac13\times105=35\text{ cm}^3$. (b) $60=\tfrac13\times20\times h \Rightarrow h = \dfrac{60\times3}{20}=9$ cm.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Q1: A pyramid has a rectangular base $5\text{ cm}\times4\text{ cm}$ and (vertical) height 6 cm; find its volume. Q2: A pyramid has base area $50\text{ cm}^2$ and height 8 cm; find its volume. Q3: A tetrahedron has a right-angled triangular base: one side next to the right angle is 6 cm and the hypotenuse of the base is 10 cm. Its apex is directly above the right-angle vertex, at a vertical height of 8 cm. Find its volume. Q4: A pyramid has a rectangular base measuring 7 cm by 6 cm and a perpendicular height of 5 cm; find its volume.
exercises.full_solution: Each uses $V=\tfrac13\times\text{base area}\times h$. Q1: $\tfrac13\times(5\times4)\times6=\tfrac13\times120=40\text{ cm}^3$. Q2: $\tfrac13\times50\times8=\tfrac{400}{3}=133.33\text{ cm}^3$. Q3: the other side next to the right angle is $\sqrt{10^2-6^2}=8$ cm, so the base area is $\tfrac12\times6\times8=24\text{ cm}^2$ and $V=\tfrac13\times24\times8=64\text{ cm}^3$. Q4: base area $=7\times6=42\text{ cm}^2$, so $V=\tfrac13\times42\times5=70\text{ cm}^3$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A pyramid has volume $168\text{ cm}^3$ and a rectangular base measuring $9\text{ cm}\times8\text{ cm}$. Calculate its height.
exercises.full_solution: Base area $=9\times8=72\text{ cm}^2$. $V=\tfrac13\times\text{base area}\times h \Rightarrow h=\dfrac{3V}{\text{base area}}=\dfrac{3\times168}{72}=7$ cm.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A pyramid has a vertical edge of $7\text{ cm}$ standing on a right-angled triangular base. In the base, one side next to the right angle is $3\text{ cm}$ and the hypotenuse is $x\text{ cm}$. The volume of the pyramid is $14\text{ cm}^3$. Calculate $x$.
exercises.full_solution: Let the unknown side next to the right angle in the base be $b$ cm. Volume $=\tfrac13\times\left(\tfrac12\times3\times b\right)\times7=3.5b$. So $3.5b=14$, giving $b=4$ cm. The edge $x$ is the hypotenuse of the base: $x=\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=\sqrt{25}=5$ cm.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A square pyramid of base edge 12 cm has its top cut off by a plane parallel to the base, forming a smaller similar pyramid of base edge 3 cm sitting on top; the remaining piece (the frustum) has height 6 cm. Since the small pyramid is similar to the original with linear scale factor $3/12=1/4$, its height is $\tfrac14$ of the original pyramid's height $H$, so $H - \tfrac14 H = 6$. Calculate: (a) the height $H$ of the original (complete) pyramid; (b) the volume of the original pyramid; (c) the volume of the frustum.
exercises.answer: (a) $H=8$ cm (b) Volume of original $=384\text{ cm}^3$ (c) Volume of frustum $=378\text{ cm}^3$
exercises.full_solution: (a) $H-\tfrac14H=6 \Rightarrow \tfrac34H=6 \Rightarrow H=8$ cm. (b) Volume of original pyramid $=\tfrac13\times12^2\times8=\tfrac13\times1152=384\text{ cm}^3$. (c) Small pyramid height $=\tfrac14\times8=2$ cm; its volume $=\tfrac13\times3^2\times2=6\text{ cm}^3$. Volume of frustum $=384-6=378\text{ cm}^3$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: The square pyramid of base edge 12 cm with its top cut off: the frustum is 6 cm high and the small pyramid removed has base edge 3 cm.

exercises.statement: A tetrahedron (a pyramid with an equilateral triangular base) has base edge $10$ cm and vertical height $12$ cm. A plane parallel to the base cuts off the top, leaving a smaller similar pyramid of base edge $5$ cm above the cut and a frustum below it. Calculate: (a) the linear scale factor $k$ of the small pyramid, and its height; (b) the volume of the small pyramid; (c) the volume of the original pyramid; (d) the volume of the frustum. Give answers correct to $3$ significant figures where they are not exact.
exercises.full_solution: Base area: the equilateral triangle of edge $10$ cm has perpendicular height $\sqrt{10^2-5^2}=\sqrt{75}\approx8.660$ cm, so its area is $\tfrac12\times10\times8.660\approx43.30\text{ cm}^2$. (a) $k=\dfrac{5}{10}=\tfrac12$, so the small pyramid's height $=\tfrac12\times12=6$ cm (the $6$ cm marked on the figure). (b) The small base is $k^2$ of the original: $\tfrac14\times43.30\approx10.83\text{ cm}^2$, so its volume $=\tfrac13\times10.83\times6\approx21.65\approx21.7\text{ cm}^3$. (c) Original volume $=\tfrac13\times43.30\times12\approx173.21\approx173\text{ cm}^3$. (d) Frustum $=173.21-21.65\approx151.55\approx152\text{ cm}^3$. Check with the volume scale factor: $k^3=\tfrac18$, and $\tfrac18\times173.21\approx21.65$, which agrees with (b).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: The tetrahedron of base edge 10 cm and height 12 cm, cut parallel to the base: the small pyramid removed has base edge 5 cm and height 6 cm, so the scale factor is a half.

exercises.statement: A regular tetrahedron (a pyramid with 4 equilateral-triangle faces) has edge length 2 cm. Calculate its total surface area, in exact ($\sqrt3$) form and to 3 s.f.
exercises.full_solution: Area of one equilateral triangle of side $s$: $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}s^2$. For $s=2$: $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}\times4=\sqrt3\text{ cm}^2$. There are 4 identical faces, so total surface area $=4\sqrt3\approx6.93\text{ cm}^2$ (3 s.f.).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A pyramid has a rectangular base $8\text{ cm}\times5\text{ cm}$, and all four slant edges (from each base corner to the apex) are 12 cm. Calculate the total surface area of the pyramid.
exercises.full_solution: For the two triangular faces on the 8 cm sides, the slant height (apex to midpoint of the 8 cm edge) is $\sqrt{12^2-4^2}=\sqrt{128}=8\sqrt2\approx11.31$ cm (each of these faces is an isosceles triangle with sides $12$, $12$ and $8$, and its height splits the $8\text{ cm}$ base into two halves of $4\text{ cm}$). Each such face has area $\tfrac12\times8\times11.31\approx45.25\text{ cm}^2$, so both together $\approx90.51\text{ cm}^2$. For the two triangular faces on the 5 cm sides, the slant height is $\sqrt{12^2-2.5^2}=\sqrt{137.75}\approx11.74$ cm, giving each face area $\tfrac12\times5\times11.74\approx29.34\text{ cm}^2$, so both together $\approx58.68\text{ cm}^2$. Base area $=8\times5=40\text{ cm}^2$. Total surface area $\approx40+90.51+58.68\approx189\text{ cm}^2$ (3 s.f.).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: (a) Calculate the volume of a cone of radius 4 cm and height 8 cm, giving your answer to 3 s.f. (b) A cone is formed by rolling up a flat sector of angle $280°$ and radius (slant height) 12 cm. Calculate (i) the arc length of the sector (which becomes the circumference of the cone's base), in exact form; (ii) the base radius of the cone, in exact form; (iii) the height of the cone, in exact form; (iv) the volume of the cone, to 3 s.f.
exercises.answer: (a) $134\text{ cm}^3$ (3 s.f.). (b)(i) $\tfrac{56}{3}\pi$ cm (ii) $\tfrac{28}{3}$ cm (iii) $\tfrac{16\sqrt2}{3}$ cm (iv) $688\text{ cm}^3$ (3 s.f.)
exercises.full_solution: (a) $V=\tfrac13\pi r^2h=\tfrac13\pi\times16\times8=\tfrac{128}{3}\pi\approx134\text{ cm}^3$. (b)(i) Arc length $=\tfrac{280}{360}\times2\pi\times12=\tfrac{56}{3}\pi$ cm. (ii) This arc becomes the base circumference, so $2\pi r_{base}=\tfrac{56}{3}\pi \Rightarrow r_{base}=\tfrac{28}{3}$ cm. (iii) Using the slant height $l=12$ as the hypotenuse: $h=\sqrt{l^2-r_{base}^2}=\sqrt{144-(28/3)^2}=\tfrac{16\sqrt2}{3}$ cm. (iv) $V=\tfrac13\pi r_{base}^2h=\tfrac13\pi\times(28/3)^2\times\tfrac{16\sqrt2}{3}\approx688\text{ cm}^3$ (3 s.f.).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Q1: Calculate the volume of a cone (to 3 s.f.) with (a) radius 3 cm, height 6 cm (b) radius 6 cm, height 7 cm (c) radius 8 mm, height 2 cm (give the answer in mm$^3$) (d) radius 6 cm, height 44 mm (give the answer in cm$^3$). Q2: Calculate the radius of a cone (to 3 s.f.) given volume $V$ and height $h$: (a) $V=600\text{ cm}^3, h=12\text{ cm}$ (b) $V=225\text{ cm}^3, h=18\text{ mm}$ (c) $V=1400\text{ mm}^3, h=2\text{ cm}$ (d) $V=0.04\text{ m}^3, h=145\text{ mm}$.
exercises.full_solution: Q1 uses $V=\tfrac13\pi r^2h$ directly, converting units where mixed (e.g. (c) $h=2\text{ cm}=20\text{ mm}$; (d) $h=44\text{ mm}=4.4\text{ cm}$). Q2 rearranges to $r=\sqrt{3V/(\pi h)}$, again converting to consistent units first (e.g. (b) $h=18\text{ mm}=1.8\text{ cm}$, so $r=\sqrt{\dfrac{3\times225}{\pi\times1.8}}\approx10.9$ cm).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A cone's base has circumference $C$ and the cone has slant height $l$. Calculate the base radius, the (vertical) height, and the volume (to 3 s.f.) for: (a) $C=50\text{ cm}, l=15\text{ cm}$ (b) $C=100\text{ cm}, l=18\text{ cm}$ (c) $C=0.4\text{ m}, l=75\text{ mm}$ (d) $C=240\text{ mm}, l=6\text{ cm}$.
exercises.full_solution: For each part: $r=C/(2\pi)$, then $h=\sqrt{l^2-r^2}$ (Pythagoras, with $l$ as the slant/hypotenuse), then $V=\tfrac13\pi r^2h$ — after converting all given lengths to the same unit first.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Cone $A$ has slant height 15 cm and base radius 5 cm. Cone $B$ has the same volume as cone $A$, and its base circumference is 60 cm. Calculate the height of cone $B$, to 3 s.f.
exercises.full_solution: For cone $A$: height $h_A=\sqrt{15^2-5^2}=\sqrt{200}=14.14$ cm, so $V_A=\tfrac13\pi\times5^2\times14.14\approx370.2\text{ cm}^3$. For cone $B$: $r_B=60/(2\pi)=9.549$ cm. Setting $V_B=V_A$: $\tfrac13\pi r_B^2h_B=370.2 \Rightarrow h_B=\dfrac{3\times370.2}{\pi\times9.549^2}\approx3.88$ cm.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A cone is formed by rolling up a sector of angle $210°$ and radius (slant height) 9 cm. Calculate, in exact form unless stated otherwise: (a) the arc length of the sector (the cone's base circumference); (b) the base radius; (c) the (vertical) height; (d) the volume, to 3 s.f.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Arc length $=\tfrac{210}{360}\times2\pi\times9=\tfrac{21}{2}\pi$ cm. (b) Base radius $r=\dfrac{\text{arc}}{2\pi}=\dfrac{21\pi/2}{2\pi}=5.25$ cm. (c) Height $h=\sqrt{9^2-\left(\tfrac{21}{4}\right)^2}=\sqrt{81-\tfrac{441}{16}}=\sqrt{\tfrac{855}{16}}=\dfrac{3\sqrt{95}}{4}\approx7.31$ cm. (d) $V=\tfrac13\pi\times5.25^2\times7.31\approx211\text{ cm}^3$ (3 s.f.).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A cone of base diameter 12 cm (radius 6 cm) and height 16 cm sits inside a cuboid box with a square base of side 12 cm and height 16 cm, touching the box on all sides. Calculate the volume of empty space inside the box (i.e. the box's volume minus the cone's volume).
exercises.full_solution: Volume of cuboid $=12\times12\times16=2304\text{ cm}^3$. Volume of cone $=\tfrac13\pi\times6^2\times16=192\pi\approx603.2\text{ cm}^3$. Empty space $=2304-603.2\approx1700\text{ cm}^3$ (3 s.f.).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: A front view of the cone of radius 6 cm and height 16 cm inside the box; the empty space is the box minus the cone.

exercises.statement: Two similar cones are formed by rolling up two sectors of the same angle $260°$, one of radius 6 cm and one of radius 9 cm. Calculate the ratio of their volumes.
exercises.full_solution: Since both cones are formed from sectors of the same angle, they are similar solids with linear scale factor $9/6=3/2$. The ratio of their volumes is the cube of the linear scale factor: $(3/2)^3=27/8$, i.e. $27:8$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: An ice cream consists of a hemisphere of radius $2.5\text{ cm}$ on top of a cone of the same radius. The total height of the ice cream (from the tip of the cone to the top of the hemisphere) is $10\text{ cm}$. Calculate, in exact form, its total volume.
exercises.full_solution:
The hemisphere's height is its radius, $2.5$ cm, so the cone's height is $10-2.5=7.5$ cm.
Volume of hemisphere $=\tfrac23\pi\times2.5^3=\dfrac{125}{12}\pi\text{ cm}^3$.
Volume of cone $=\tfrac13\pi\times2.5^2\times7.5=\dfrac{125}{8}\pi\text{ cm}^3$.
Total $=\dfrac{125}{12}\pi+\dfrac{125}{8}\pi=\dfrac{250+375}{24}\pi=\dfrac{625}{24}\pi\approx81.8\text{ cm}^3$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A solid consists of a cylinder of diameter 8 m (radius 4 m) and height 12 m, topped by a cone of the same radius 4 m and height 10 m. Calculate the total volume of the solid.
exercises.full_solution: Volume of cone $=\tfrac13\pi\times4^2\times10\approx167.55\text{ m}^3$. Volume of cylinder $=\pi\times4^2\times12\approx603.19\text{ m}^3$. Total $\approx167.55+603.19\approx771\text{ m}^3$ (3 s.f.).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A solid is made of two identical frustums joined at their narrow ('waist') ends. The overall length is 36 cm; each of the two wide ends has diameter 16 cm (radius 8 cm), and the narrow waist has diameter 4 cm (radius 2 cm), so each frustum has length 18 cm. Calculate the total volume of the solid, in terms of $\pi$.
exercises.full_solution:
Each frustum is part of a cone. Complete one frustum into a full cone of height $H$: the cut-off cone (radius $2$ cm) is similar to the full cone (radius $8$ cm) with scale factor $\tfrac28=\tfrac14$, so its height is $\tfrac14H$ and $H-\tfrac14H=18$, giving $H=24$ cm (small cone height $6$ cm).
Volume of one frustum $=\tfrac13\pi\times8^2\times24-\tfrac13\pi\times2^2\times6=512\pi-8\pi=504\pi\text{ cm}^3$.
Total for both frustums $=2\times504\pi=1008\pi\text{ cm}^3\approx3170\text{ cm}^3$ (3 s.f.).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

assets.caption: The solid made of two identical frustums joined at the 4 cm waist, each 18 cm long with a wide end of diameter 16 cm.

exercises.statement: Two cones $A$ and $B$ are placed either end of a cylindrical tube of diameter $10\text{ cm}$ (radius $5\text{ cm}$). Each cone's base fills one end of the tube, and the two apexes meet at a point inside the tube. Cone $A$ is $25\text{ cm}$ long. Given that the volumes of $A$ and $B$ are in the ratio $2:1$, calculate: (a) the volume of cone $A$; (b) the height of cone $B$; (c) the volume of the cylinder.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) $V_A=\tfrac13\pi\times5^2\times25=\dfrac{625}{3}\pi\approx654\text{ cm}^3$.
(b) Both cones have the same radius, so their volumes are proportional to their heights. $V_A:V_B=2:1$, so $h_B=\tfrac12\times25=12.5$ cm.
(c) The tube's length is $h_A+h_B=25+12.5=37.5$ cm, so $V=\pi\times5^2\times37.5=937.5\pi\approx2950\text{ cm}^3$.
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: A cone has base radius 5 cm and slant height 12 cm. Calculate its total surface area, to 3 s.f.
exercises.full_solution: Base area $=\pi r^2=\pi\times25=25\pi\text{ cm}^2$. The curved surface, when unrolled, is a sector of radius 12 (the slant height) whose arc length equals the base circumference $2\pi\times5=10\pi$. The sector's angle is $\phi=\dfrac{10\pi}{2\pi\times12}\times360=150°$. Sector (curved surface) area $=\tfrac{150}{360}\times\pi\times12^2=60\pi\text{ cm}^2$. Total surface area $=25\pi+60\pi=85\pi\approx267\text{ cm}^2$ (3 s.f.).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)
exercises.source_label: Worked example (surface area of a cone)

exercises.statement: Calculate the total surface area of each cone, to 3 s.f.: (a) slant height $16$ cm, base radius $6$ cm; (b) slant height $20$ cm, base radius $15$ cm.
exercises.full_solution: Total surface area $=\pi r^2+\pi rl$ (base + curved surface). (a) $\pi\times6^2+\pi\times6\times16=36\pi+96\pi=132\pi\approx415\text{ cm}^2$. (b) $\pi\times15^2+\pi\times15\times20=225\pi+300\pi=525\pi\approx1650\text{ cm}^2$ (3 s.f.).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exercises.statement: Two cones with the same base radius of $8\text{ cm}$ are stuck together base to base (the shared base is inside the shape). One cone has slant height $15$ cm and the other has slant height $30$ cm. Calculate the surface area of the shape, in terms of $\pi$.
exercises.full_solution: The shared base is inside the shape, so the surface area is the sum of the two curved surfaces: $\pi rl_1+\pi rl_2=\pi\times8\times15+\pi\times8\times30=120\pi+240\pi=360\pi\text{ cm}^2\approx1130\text{ cm}^2$ (3 s.f.).
exercises.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: The end wall of a house is shaped like a rectangle of width 15 m and height 4 m, topped by a triangular gable of base 15 m and perpendicular height 4 m. Calculate the total area of the end wall.
exam_questions.full_solution: Area of rectangle $=15\times4=60\text{ m}^2$. Area of triangle $=\tfrac12\times15\times4=30\text{ m}^2$. Total area $=60+30=90\text{ m}^2$.

M1 for area of triangle = 30
A1 for total area = 90 m²

exam_questions.statement: Calculate, to 3 significant figures: (a) the circumference and area of a circle of radius 5.5 cm; (b) the circumference and area of a circle of diameter 16 mm.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) Radius $=5.5$ cm. $C=2\pi\times5.5=34.6$ cm (3 s.f.); $A=\pi\times5.5^2=95.0\text{ cm}^2$ (3 s.f.). (b) Diameter 16 mm $\Rightarrow$ radius $=8$ mm. $C=2\pi\times8=50.3$ mm (3 s.f.); $A=\pi\times8^2=201\text{ mm}^2$ (3 s.f.).
mark_scheme: M1 for identifying radius correctly in each part
A1 for C = 34.6 cm (a)
A1 for A = 95.0 cm² (a)
A1 for C = 50.3 mm and A = 201 mm² (b)
