exam_questions.statement: A shape is formed by cutting a semicircle of radius 3 cm out of one side of a $6\text{ cm}\times4\text{ cm}$ rectangle (the semicircle's diameter, 6 cm, coincides with one full side of the rectangle). Calculate the shaded (remaining) area, giving your answer in terms of $\pi$ and also to 3 significant figures.
exam_questions.full_solution: Area of rectangle $=6\times4=24\text{ cm}^2$. Area of semicircle $=\tfrac12\pi\times3^2=4.5\pi\text{ cm}^2$. Shaded area $=24-4.5\pi\approx9.86\text{ cm}^2$ (3 s.f.).
mark_scheme: M1 for rectangle area = 24
M1 for semicircle area = 4.5π (using radius 3)
A1 for exact answer 24 - 4.5π
A1 for 9.86 cm² to 3 s.f.
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: A shape is made of three parts, one above the other: a parallelogram at the top (top side $7\text{ cm}$, height $4\text{ cm}$), a trapezium in the middle (parallel sides $7\text{ cm}$ and $10\text{ cm}$, height $4\text{ cm}$) and a semicircle of radius $5\text{ cm}$ at the bottom, whose diameter is the $10\text{ cm}$ side of the trapezium. Calculate the area of: (a) the semicircle, (b) the trapezium, (c) the whole shape. Give your answers to 3 significant figures where appropriate.
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a) Semicircle: $\tfrac12\pi\times5^2=12.5\pi\approx39.3\text{ cm}^2$.
(b) Trapezium: $\tfrac12\times4\times(7+10)=34\text{ cm}^2$.
(c) Parallelogram: $7\times4=28\text{ cm}^2$. Whole shape $=28+34+39.27\approx101\text{ cm}^2$ (3 s.f.).
mark_scheme: M1 for semicircle area $=\tfrac12\pi\times5^2$
A1 for (a) $12.5\pi\approx39.3\text{ cm}^2$
B1 for (b) trapezium area $=34\text{ cm}^2$
B1 for (c) total $=28+34+39.3\approx101\text{ cm}^2$ (including the parallelogram $7\times4=28$)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: A length of pipe can be modelled as a hollow cylinder of inner radius 3 cm, outer radius 3.5 cm, and length 15 cm. Calculate, to 3 significant figures: (a) the cross-sectional (annular) area at each end of the pipe; (b) the total surface area of the pipe's inner surface; (c) the total surface area of the whole pipe (inner curved surface + outer curved surface + the two annular end faces).
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) Cross-sectional area $=\pi(3.5^2-3^2)=\pi(12.25-9)=3.25\pi\text{ cm}^2$. (b) Inner curved surface area $=2\pi\times3\times15=90\pi\text{ cm}^2$. (c) Outer curved surface area $=2\pi\times3.5\times15=105\pi\text{ cm}^2$. Total surface area $=2\times3.25\pi+90\pi+105\pi=6.5\pi+90\pi+105\pi=201.5\pi\text{ cm}^2\approx633\text{ cm}^2$ (3 s.f.).
mark_scheme: M1 for cross-sectional (annular) area formula π(R² - r²)
A1 for (a) = 3.25π
M1 for inner curved surface area = 2πrl
A1 for (b) = 90π
M1 for outer curved surface area and summing all 4 surfaces (2 ends + inner + outer)
A1 for (c) = 201.5π cm² (≈ 633 cm²)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: Calculate the volume of a cylinder with: (a) radius 3 mm and height 12 mm; (b) radius 1.25 cm and height 2 cm. Give both answers in terms of $\pi$.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) $V=\pi r^2h=\pi\times3^2\times12=108\pi\approx339\text{ mm}^3$ (3 s.f.). (b) $V=\pi\times1.25^2\times2=3.125\pi\approx9.82\text{ cm}^3$ (3 s.f.).
mark_scheme: M1 for V = πr²h applied correctly in (a)
A1 for (a) = 108π mm³ (≈ 339 mm³)
M1 for V = πr²h applied correctly in (b)
A1 for (b) = 3.125π cm³ (≈ 9.82 cm³)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: Calculate the arc length, to 3 significant figures, of a sector with: (a) angle $45°$ and radius 15 cm; (b) angle $150°$ and radius 13.5 cm.
exam_questions.full_solution: Arc length $=\tfrac{\theta}{360}\times2\pi r$. (a) $\tfrac{45}{360}\times2\pi\times15=11.8$ cm (3 s.f.). (b) $\tfrac{150}{360}\times2\pi\times13.5=35.3$ cm (3 s.f.).
mark_scheme: M1 for correct substitution into arc length formula (a)
A1 for 11.8 cm (a)
M1 for correct substitution into arc length formula (b)
A1 for 35.3 cm (b)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: Calculate the angle subtended at the centre, to the nearest degree, for a sector with: (a) radius 20 mm and arc length 95 mm; (b) radius 9 cm and arc length 9 mm.
exam_questions.full_solution: $\theta=\dfrac{\text{arc}}{2\pi r}\times360$. (a) $\dfrac{95}{2\pi\times20}\times360\approx272°$. (b) Converting to consistent units, $r=9\text{ cm}=90\text{ mm}$, arc $=9$ mm: $\dfrac{9}{2\pi\times90}\times360\approx6°$.
mark_scheme: M1 for correct rearrangement of arc length formula to find θ (a)
M1 for unit conversion and correct substitution (b)
A1 for ≈6° (b)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: Calculate the area of a sector of angle $40°$ and radius 18 cm, giving your answer in terms of $\pi$.
exam_questions.full_solution: Sector area $=\tfrac{\theta}{360}\times\pi r^2=\tfrac{40}{360}\times\pi\times18^2=\tfrac19\times324\pi=36\pi\text{ cm}^2\approx113\text{ cm}^2$ (3 s.f.).
mark_scheme: M1 for correct substitution into sector area formula
A1 for 36π cm² (≈113 cm²)
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: A sphere has radius 6.5 cm. Calculate: (a) its surface area, to 3 significant figures; (b) its volume, to 3 significant figures.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) $SA=4\pi r^2=4\pi\times6.5^2\approx531\text{ cm}^2$ (3 s.f.). (b) $V=\tfrac43\pi r^3=\tfrac43\pi\times6.5^3\approx1150\text{ cm}^3$ (3 s.f.).
mark_scheme: M1 for SA = 4πr² substituted correctly
A1 for 531 cm²
M1 for V = (4/3)πr³ substituted correctly
A1 for 1150 cm³
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: A regular hexagonal pyramid has a base edge of 12 cm and each slant (sloping) edge from a base vertex to the apex measures 24 cm. Calculate: (a) the vertical height of the pyramid; (b) the total surface area of the pyramid; (c) the volume of the pyramid. Give your answers to 3 significant figures where appropriate.
exam_questions.full_solution: For a regular hexagon of side $s=12$ cm, the circumradius (centre to vertex) equals the side length, $R=12$ cm. (a) The slant edge (apex to base vertex) is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with the vertical height $H$ and the circumradius $R=12$: $H=\sqrt{24^2-12^2}=\sqrt{432}\approx20.8$ cm. (b) The hexagon's apothem (centre to edge midpoint) is $a=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\times12\approx10.39$ cm. The slant height of each triangular face (apex to base-edge midpoint) is $l=\sqrt{H^2+a^2}=\sqrt{20.78^2+10.39^2}\approx23.24$ cm. Base area $=6\times\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}\times12^2\approx374.1\text{ cm}^2$. Each triangular face area $=\tfrac12\times12\times23.24\approx139.4\text{ cm}^2$, so 6 faces $\approx836.6\text{ cm}^2$. Total surface area $\approx374.1+836.6\approx1210\text{ cm}^2$ (3 s.f.). (c) $V=\tfrac13\times\text{base area}\times H\approx\tfrac13\times374.1\times20.78\approx2590\text{ cm}^3$ (3 s.f.).
mark_scheme: M1 for recognising circumradius of hexagon = side length (12 cm)
M1 for H = sqrt(24² - 12²) using Pythagoras
A1 for H ≈ 20.8 cm
M1 for apothem = (√3/2)×12
M1 for slant height of a face via Pythagoras with H and apothem
A1 for total surface area ≈ 1210 cm²
M1 for volume = (1/3) × base area × H
A1 for volume ≈ 2590 cm³
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: A prism has length 8 cm, and its cross-section is a sector of a circle with angle $50°$ and arc length 20 cm. Calculate: (a) the radius of the sector; (b) the cross-sectional area of the prism; (c) the total surface area of the prism; (d) the volume of the prism. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
exam_questions.answer: (a) $r \approx 22.9$ cm (b) cross-sectional area $\approx 229\text{ cm}^2$ (c) total surface area $\approx 985\text{ cm}^2$ (d) volume $\approx 1830\text{ cm}^3$
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) Arc length $=\tfrac{\theta}{360}\times2\pi r \Rightarrow r=\dfrac{20\times360}{50\times2\pi}\approx22.92$ cm. (b) Cross-sectional (sector) area $=\tfrac{50}{360}\times\pi\times22.92^2\approx229\text{ cm}^2$. (c) Perimeter of the sector cross-section $=20+2\times22.92\approx65.84$ cm. Total surface area $=2\times(\text{cross-sectional area})+(\text{perimeter})\times(\text{length})\approx2\times229+65.84\times8\approx458+526.7\approx985\text{ cm}^2$. (d) Volume $=\text{cross-sectional area}\times\text{length}\approx229\times8\approx1830\text{ cm}^3$.
mark_scheme: M1 for rearranging arc length formula to find r
A1 for r ≈ 22.9 cm
M1 for sector area formula applied with found r
A1 for cross-sectional area ≈ 229 cm²
M1 for perimeter of sector = arc + 2r, and total SA = 2(area) + perimeter × length
A1 for total surface area ≈ 985 cm²
M1 for volume = cross-sectional area × length
A1 for volume ≈ 1830 cm³
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: A sphere of radius 6 cm has the same volume as a cone of height 6 cm. Calculate: (a) the base radius of the cone; (b) the total surface area of the cone, to 3 significant figures.
exam_questions.full_solution: Volume of sphere $=\tfrac43\pi\times6^3=288\pi\text{ cm}^3$. (a) Setting this equal to the cone's volume: $\tfrac13\pi r^2\times6=288\pi \Rightarrow r^2=\dfrac{288\times3}{6}=144 \Rightarrow r=12$ cm. (b) Slant height of the cone $=\sqrt{12^2+6^2}=\sqrt{180}=6\sqrt5\approx13.42$ cm. Total surface area $=\pi r^2+\pi rl=\pi\times144+\pi\times12\times13.42\approx452.4+505.9\approx958\text{ cm}^2$ (3 s.f.).
mark_scheme: M1 for volume of sphere = (4/3)π(6)³ = 288π
M1 for setting cone volume (1/3)πr²(6) equal to sphere's volume
A1 for r = 12 cm
M1 for slant height via Pythagoras, l = sqrt(12²+6²)
A1 for l ≈ 13.4 cm
M1 for SA formula πr² + πrl applied correctly
A1 for total surface area ≈ 958 cm²
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement: A frustum is formed from a cone of base radius 28 mm by cutting off the top, leaving a smaller circular top face of radius 14 mm; the frustum's height is 50 mm. A cylindrical hole of radius 14 mm is then drilled all the way through the frustum, parallel to its axis, removing a cylinder of radius 14 mm and height 50 mm (the frustum's height) from its centre. Calculate: (a) the height of the original (complete, before cutting) cone; (b) the volume of the frustum (before drilling); (c) the volume of material remaining after the hole is drilled.
exam_questions.answer: (a) $H = 100$ mm (b) frustum volume $\approx 71800\text{ mm}^3$ (c) remaining volume $\approx 41100\text{ mm}^3$
exam_questions.full_solution: Since the top radius (14 mm) is half the base radius (28 mm), the small cut-off cone is similar to the original with linear scale factor $\tfrac12$, so its height is half that of the original cone. If the original cone's height is $H$, the small cone's height is $H/2$, and the frustum's height is $H - H/2 = H/2 = 50 \Rightarrow H=100$ mm. (a) $H=100$ mm. (b) Volume of original cone $=\tfrac13\pi\times28^2\times100\approx82100\text{ mm}^3$. Volume of small cone (height 50 mm, radius 14 mm) $=\tfrac13\pi\times14^2\times50\approx10267\text{ mm}^3$. Volume of frustum $=82100-10267\approx71800\text{ mm}^3$ (3 s.f.). (c) Volume of cylindrical hole $=\pi\times14^2\times50\approx30800\text{ mm}^3$. Remaining volume $=71800-30800\approx41100\text{ mm}^3$ (3 s.f.).
mark_scheme: M1 for recognising the small-cone/frustum height ratio from the radius ratio 14:28 = 1:2
A1 for H = 100 mm
M1 A1 for volume of original cone = (1/3)π(28)²(100) ≈ 82 100 mm³
M1 for volume of small cone = (1/3)π(14)²(50)
A1 for frustum volume ≈ 71800 mm³
M1 A1 for volume of cylindrical hole = π(14)²(50) ≈ 30 800 mm³
A1 for remaining volume ≈ 41100 mm³
exam_questions.source_book: Pimentel & Wall, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended (Hodder, 2018)

exam_questions.statement:
A grain store is made from a cylinder with a cone on top. The cylinder has diameter $6$ m and height $4$ m. The cone has the same radius as the cylinder and vertical height $2.5$ m.
(a) Show that the total volume of the grain store is $137\text{ m}^3$, correct to $3$ significant figures. [3]
(b) The store is filled with grain to $70\%$ of its total volume. $1\text{ m}^3$ of this grain has a mass of $0.78$ tonnes.
Calculate the mass of grain in the store, correct to the nearest tonne. [3]
(c) The curved surface of the cylinder and the curved surface of the cone are painted. One tin of paint covers $12\text{ m}^2$.
Work out the number of tins needed. You must show all your working. [4]
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a) The radius is $6\div2=3$ m. Cylinder: $V=\pi\times3^2\times4=36\pi=113.097\ldots\text{ m}^3$. Cone: $V=\tfrac13\pi\times3^2\times2.5=7.5\pi=23.561\ldots\text{ m}^3$. Total $=43.5\pi=136.659\ldots=137\text{ m}^3$ (3 s.f.), as required.
(b) Volume of grain $=0.70\times136.659\ldots=95.661\ldots\text{ m}^3$. Mass $=95.661\ldots\times0.78=74.615\ldots=75$ tonnes (nearest tonne).
(c) Slant height of the cone: $l=\sqrt{3^2+2.5^2}=\sqrt{15.25}=3.905\ldots$ m. Curved surface of cone $=\pi r l=\pi\times3\times3.905\ldots=36.80\ldots\text{ m}^2$. Curved surface of cylinder $=2\pi r h=2\pi\times3\times4=24\pi=75.39\ldots\text{ m}^2$. Total area to paint $=112.2\text{ m}^2$ (3 s.f.). Tins $=112.2\div12=9.35\ldots$, so $10$ tins must be bought.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for $\pi\times3^2\times4$ (or $36\pi$, or $113.1$); M1 for $\tfrac13\pi\times3^2\times2.5$ (or $7.5\pi$, or $23.6$); A1 for $136.6\ldots$ seen before the rounding to $137\text{ m}^3$ (a bare $137$ with no unrounded value does not earn the final mark on a 'show that' question)
(b) M1 for $0.70\times$ their total volume (or $95.7$); M1 for multiplying their volume of grain by $0.78$; A1 for $75$ tonnes

(c) M1 for the slant height $\sqrt{3^2+2.5^2}=3.905\ldots$; M1 for the curved surface of the cone $\pi\times3\times$ their $l$ (or $36.8$); M1 for the curved surface of the cylinder $2\pi\times3\times4$ (or $75.4$) added to their cone area; A1 for $10$ tins (an answer of $9$ or $9.35$ scores no final mark, because part tins cannot be bought)
common_errors: Using the diameter $6$ m as the radius in both volume formulas, which multiplies every answer by $4$.
In (c), using the vertical height $2.5$ m in $\pi r l$ instead of the slant height $3.905\ldots$ m.
In (c), including the circular base of the cylinder, or the base of the cone, when only the two curved surfaces are painted; or rounding $9.35$ down to $9$ tins.

exam_questions.statement:
A wooden toy is a solid cone joined to a solid hemisphere (half a sphere). Both have radius $5$ cm and the vertical height of the cone is $12$ cm. The flat face of the hemisphere is joined to the base of the cone, so no flat surface of the toy is exposed.
(a) Show that the slant height of the cone is $13$ cm. [1]
(b) Find the total surface area of the toy, giving your answer in terms of $\pi$. [3]
(c) Calculate the volume of the toy, correct to $3$ significant figures. [3]
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a) By Pythagoras' theorem, $l=\sqrt{5^2+12^2}=\sqrt{25+144}=\sqrt{169}=13$ cm, as required.
(b) Curved surface of the cone $=\pi r l=\pi\times5\times13=65\pi\,\text{cm}^2$. Curved surface of the hemisphere is half the surface area of a sphere, $\tfrac12\times4\pi r^2=2\pi\times5^2=50\pi\,\text{cm}^2$. Total $=65\pi+50\pi=115\pi\,\text{cm}^2$.
(c) Cone: $V=\tfrac13\pi r^2h=\tfrac13\pi\times5^2\times12=100\pi\,\text{cm}^3$. Hemisphere: $V=\tfrac12\times\tfrac43\pi r^3=\tfrac23\pi\times5^3=\tfrac{250\pi}{3}\,\text{cm}^3$. Total $=100\pi+\tfrac{250\pi}{3}=\tfrac{550\pi}{3}=575.95\ldots=576\text{ cm}^3$ (3 s.f.).
mark_scheme: (a) B1 for $\sqrt{5^2+12^2}=13$ (or for quoting the $5,12,13$ right-angled triangle)
(b) M1 for the curved surface of the cone $\pi\times5\times13$ (or $65\pi$); M1 for the curved surface of the hemisphere $2\pi\times5^2$ (or $50\pi$); A1 for $115\pi\,\text{cm}^2$
(c) M1 for $\tfrac13\pi\times5^2\times12$ (or $100\pi$); M1 for $\tfrac23\pi\times5^3$ (or $\tfrac{250\pi}{3}$, or $262$); A1 for $576\text{ cm}^3$
common_errors: In (b), using the full sphere surface area $4\pi r^2=100\pi$ for the hemisphere instead of half of it, $2\pi r^2=50\pi$.
In (b), adding the circular base of the cone: that face is joined to the hemisphere, so it is not part of the surface of the toy.
In (c), using the whole sphere volume $\tfrac43\pi r^3$, or using the slant height $13$ cm in place of the vertical height $12$ cm in the cone volume.

exam_questions.statement:
A window has the shape of a rectangle of width $1.2$ m and height $1.8$ m, with a semicircle of diameter $1.2$ m on top.
(a) Show that the area of the window is $2.73\text{ m}^2$, correct to $3$ significant figures. [3]
(b) A strip of sealant is fitted all the way round the outside edge of the window.
Calculate the length of the strip needed, correct to $3$ significant figures. [3]
(c) The glass for the window costs $\$45$ per square metre.
Calculate the cost of the glass, correct to the nearest dollar. [2]
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a) Rectangle: $1.2\times1.8=2.16\text{ m}^2$. The semicircle has radius $1.2\div2=0.6$ m, so its area is $\tfrac12\pi\times0.6^2=0.18\pi=0.5654\ldots\text{ m}^2$. Total $=2.16+0.5654\ldots=2.7254\ldots=2.73\text{ m}^2$ (3 s.f.), as required.
(b) The outside edge is the bottom of the rectangle, its two vertical sides and the semicircular arc. The $1.2$ m line where the semicircle meets the rectangle is inside the window, so it is not included. Straight parts: $1.2+1.8+1.8=4.8$ m. Arc: $\tfrac12\times2\pi\times0.6=\pi\times0.6=1.8849\ldots$ m. Total $=4.8+1.8849\ldots=6.6849\ldots=6.69$ m (3 s.f.).
(c) Cost $=2.7254\ldots\times45=122.64\ldots$, so the glass costs $\$123$ to the nearest dollar.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for $1.2\times1.8=2.16$; M1 for $\tfrac12\pi\times0.6^2$ (or $0.18\pi$, or $0.565$) using radius $0.6$; A1 for $2.725\ldots$ seen before the rounding to $2.73\text{ m}^2$
(b) M1 for the semicircular arc $\pi\times0.6$ (or $1.88$); M1 for the three straight sides $1.2+1.8+1.8=4.8$ (the $1.2$ m join is correctly excluded); A1 for $6.69$ m
(c) M1 for their area $\times45$; A1 for $\$123$
common_errors: Using $1.2$ m as the radius of the semicircle instead of $0.6$ m.
In (b), using $2\pi r=1.2\pi$ for the arc (the whole circumference) rather than half of it.
In (b), adding the $1.2$ m line between the rectangle and the semicircle, which is not part of the outside edge.

summary.big_idea: Use the key mathematical ideas and methods from mensuration accurately in mixed practice and exam-style problems.
